verdicts.title: Error taxonomy incomplete: 500/529/timeout/connection errors crash instead of backoff/fallback
verdicts.reasoning:
Every load-bearing technical assertion verified against the code and installed litellm 1.85.0.

1. Comment/code mismatch confirmed. /Users/cyan/ccr/know-expand/know_expand/agents/base.py:726-727 says the counter is "for headerless 429/500/529", but both handlers (lines 750-751 in call(), 901-902 in call_with_tools()) only do _find_in_chain(e, litellm.RateLimitError) and _find_in_chain(e, litellm.ServiceUnavailableError). _find_in_chain uses isinstance (base.py:394-403), and in litellm 1.85.0 InternalServerError is NOT a subclass of ServiceUnavailableError (verified via MRO inspection: both descend directly from APIStatusError; issubclass returns False both directions). So 500/529 never enter the backoff path despite the comment.

2. litellm mapping confirmed. exception_mapping_utils.py in the installed venv maps Anthropic "overloaded_error"/"Overloaded" strings and status codes 500 and 529 to litellm.InternalServerError. Timeout subclasses APIConnectionError, not ServiceUnavailableError.

3. Grep confirms InternalServerError, APIConnectionError, and litellm Timeout are referenced nowhere in the know_expand package (only JS setTimeout hits in observe.py). litellm.num_retries is None (no global retry), and instructor's retry only re-asks on validation errors, so these exceptions reach the router's else branch and, for non-geminicli models, hit the bare `raise` at base.py:814 — no backoff, no model switch. This contradicts both the base.py comment and README.md:663 design principle 13.

4. Timeout claim confirmed: _do_call/_do_call_with_thinking/call_with_tools pass no timeout kwarg to litellm/instructor (only the geminicli subprocess path and a 3s httpx health probe have explicit timeouts); non-geminicli calls rely on litellm's default request_timeout.

One refinement to the impact narrative (does not reduce severity): the propagated exception does not always literally "crash a stage". S5 gathers per-domain coroutines with return_exceptions=True (s5_research.py:990-1010) and S4 has a per-domain try/except (s4_audit.py:424-432), so in those stages a transient 529 silently drops an entire domain's content, emits s5_domain_failed/domain_failed, and still marks the stage complete — meaning resume will NOT regenerate the lost domain. That is arguably worse than a crash. In S7 (gather at s7_synthesize.py:356-359 without return_exceptions), S2's main extraction call, S1, and S3 the exception is unhandled and does crash the run (pipeline.py and cli.py contain zero try/except). High severity stands either way: a single transient Anthropic overload either crashes the run mid-stage or permanently loses a domain from the final document.

verdicts.title: Retry-After path: unbounded retry loop, uncapped sleep, and int() crash on HTTP-date
verdicts.reasoning:
I tried to refute this and could not — every sub-claim matches the code, and the one mitigating factor the auditor conceded turns out not to exist.

1. Unbounded retry loop: At /Users/cyan/ccr/know-expand/know_expand/agents/base.py:764-772 (QuotaAwareRouter.call) and the duplicate at 908-915 (call_with_tools), when a RateLimitError/ServiceUnavailableError carries a `retry-after` header, the code executes `self._fail_counts.pop(model, None); await asyncio.sleep(int(retry_after)); continue`. The pop actively RESETS the 3-strike counter, the model is never added to `self._skip`, and `_next_model()` returns the same model. There is no iteration cap, no cumulative-sleep cap, and no escalation on this branch — a provider that persistently returns 429 + Retry-After (Anthropic includes retry-after on 429s; Groq free tier includes it on daily-quota exhaustion with multi-hour values, and Groq/Mistral free tiers are this repo's actual fallback providers per models.yaml/CLAUDE.md) is retried on the same model forever. README.md:667-668, 690, and 913 document the "429 without Retry-After = true exhaustion" assumption, confirming the design relies on exhausted quotas omitting the header, which is not reliably true.

2. Uncapped sleep: `int(retry_after)` is passed to asyncio.sleep with no clamp — Retry-After: 86400 stalls the coroutine for a day.

3. int() crash on HTTP-date: RFC 9110 §10.2.3 allows Retry-After to be an HTTP-date; `int("Wed, 21 Oct 2026 07:28:00 GMT")` raises ValueError inside the `except` handler, which propagates out of call() as an unrelated crash (with the original error only as __context__). No parsing helper or try/except guards it. tests/test_base.py has zero coverage of the retry-after path (grep for retry_after/RateLimitError/retry-after returns nothing).

4. Mitigation search came up worse than claimed, not better: the auditor's concession that "only S5 has an outer 2700s timeout" is itself false in the code. config.yaml has `domain_research_seconds: 2700` and README.md:752 claims "Each domain task in S5 is wrapped with asyncio.timeout(2700)", but `domain_research_seconds` is referenced by zero .py files and s5_research.py contains no asyncio.timeout/wait_for at all (the only wait_for calls in the codebase are around the geminicli subprocess at base.py:138/221). So no stage-level timeout bounds this loop anywhere.

Severity "high" is defensible for an unattended overnight pipeline: this is a liveness hang (indefinite same-model retry while working fallback models sit idle) plus an uncapped day-long sleep plus a latent ValueError crash, on the primary error-handling path of the only LLM router in the system. The only soft caveat: triggering the loop requires litellm to surface `.response.headers` on the exception (when absent, the headerless 3-strike path correctly fails over) — that is a precondition, not a refutation, since litellm's OpenAI-SDK-derived exceptions do carry the httpx response for the major providers.
verdicts.correction: Claim stands as written. One detail is wrong in the code's favor-of-the-auditor direction: the "outer 2700s timeout in S5" the claim cites as the sole bound does not actually exist in code — it is documented in README.md:752 and configured in config.yaml (`domain_research_seconds: 2700`) but never wired up in s5_research.py — so the exposure is strictly worse than claimed.

verdicts.title: geminicli subprocess provider: orphaned processes on timeout, unpinned npx supply chain, prompt in argv
verdicts.reasoning: All three cited code behaviors are real and the line numbers are exact. (1) /Users/cyan/ccr/know-expand/know_expand/agents/base.py:138-141 and 221-224 use `asyncio.wait_for(proc.communicate(), timeout=cfg.timeouts.get("geminicli_timeout_s", 120))` with no kill on timeout; the except blocks (175-185, and the tool-call equivalent) only emit an event and re-raise, and a repo-wide grep finds zero `.kill()`/`.terminate()` calls in the package — so a timed-out npx→node→gemini-cli child is indeed left running. (2) base.py:132 and 215 spawn `npx --yes @google/gemini-cli` with no version pin anywhere in the repo, and models.yaml places geminicli/gemini-3.5-flash at slot 0 for all seven roles, so it is the default routing path for every call. (3) The full prompt, built from message content including document text, is passed as `-p full_prompt` in argv (base.py:134, 217) — ps-visible and ARG_MAX-bounded; gemini-cli's stdin mode is not used. However, the impact framing of problem (1) is overstated: the auditor missed QuotaAwareRouter.call()'s else-branch at base.py:799-813, where ANY geminicli exception (including TimeoutError) permanently adds the model to that router's `_skip` set ("geminicli errors are always terminal for this run"). Routers are created per stage (make_router per stage entry), so timeouts cannot recur for hours — leaks are bounded to roughly one in-flight concurrent batch per stage before geminicli is abandoned. Additionally, gemini-cli `-p` is one-shot (leaked children usually run to completion and exit rather than persisting indefinitely), and the web UI stop path uses os.killpg (observe.py:2705), which sweeps same-process-group children on manual stop. The missing proc.kill() is still a genuine defect worth fixing, the unpinned npx and argv-prompt findings stand as written, but "accumulates orphans for hours at 8 concurrent calls" does not match the actual fallback behavior, which slightly inflates the headline severity.
verdicts.correction: The code defects are real, but the orphan-accumulation scenario is bounded, not open-ended: on the first geminicli TimeoutError, QuotaAwareRouter permanently skips geminicli for that router instance (base.py:799-813, per-stage routers), so at most one concurrent batch of calls (~8) can leak per stage per run — not continuous accumulation for hours. Leaked gemini-cli one-shot processes also typically self-terminate after completing their single request, and os.killpg on manual stop (observe.py:2705) cleans same-group survivors. Severity is closer to medium-high: the unpinned `npx --yes @google/gemini-cli` supply chain and prompt-in-argv exposure are accurately described and unmitigated.

verdicts.title: Silent model aliasing: models.yaml says gemini-3.5-flash, code runs gemini-3.1-pro-preview, README says gemini-2.5-pro
verdicts.reasoning:
Every checkable assertion in the claim is accurate against the repo.

1. Hardcoded substitution — CONFIRMED. /Users/cyan/ccr/know-expand/know_expand/agents/base.py:29 defines `_GEMINICLI_CLI_MODEL = "gemini-3.1-pro-preview"`, and `_geminicli_model_name` (base.py:42-44) takes the requested model as a parameter and unconditionally returns the hardcoded constant — the argument is discarded. Both call paths (`_do_geminicli_call` line 110, `_do_geminicli_tool_call` line 196) pass this to `npx @google/gemini-cli -m`.

2. YAML routing key names a model that never runs — CONFIRMED. models.yaml slot 0 is `"geminicli/gemini-3.5-flash"` in all six roles (lines 26, 35, 46, 58, 68, 77, 87), and the header comment (line 2) describes it as the free OAuth CLI without mentioning the actual model is 3.1-pro-preview.

3. Third name in README — CONFIRMED. README.md:701 and :1022 both reference `geminicli/gemini-2.5-pro`, a name that appears nowhere in models.yaml or code. README's models.yaml example (lines 255-281) uses `geminicli/gemini-3.5-flash`, and `gemini-3.1-pro-preview` appears nowhere in README.md at all. So three documents genuinely give three different model names for the same provider slot.

4. Dual-key mismatch already shipped a bug — CONFIRMED. Commit fd18d6e ("Fix geminicli PROBED_UNAVAILABLE key mismatch") shows `_PROBED_UNAVAILABLE.add(f"geminicli/{cli_model}")` previously added the wrong key so the global quota skip "silently never fired"; the regression test is exactly at tests/test_base.py:242-290 as cited. Events still log the CLI name (`f"geminicli/{cli_model}"` at base.py:125, 166, 180, 209) while skip-state keys on the yaml name (base.py:154, 230) — the split-key convention persists and is held together only by code comments and one test.

Two minor qualifications that temper but do not refute the claim: (a) the sentence "the system cannot truthfully state which model produced the content" is slightly overstated — events.jsonl does log the real CLI model (`geminicli/gemini-3.1-pro-preview`) in llm_call_done, and probe_models deliberately reports "the real CLI model name so the log is truthful" (base.py:483-486); run-level provenance is recoverable from the event log. (b) The aliasing is not fully silent to maintainers — CLAUDE.md:78 documents the `-m gemini-3.1-pro-preview` invocation. However, neither point rescues the user-facing surfaces: models.yaml and README — the two documents a user would read to know what model runs — name two different wrong models, and the README is internally inconsistent (3.5-flash in its example, 2.5-pro in its constraints). Severity "high" is defensible rather than inflated: this exact key-aliasing already caused one shipped runtime bug, and the convention remains a standing footgun for any new geminicli code path.

issues.title: Mandatory human interview (S1) with broken bypass makes the default pipeline human-gated — incompatible with unattended/multi-user operation
issues.detail: Design principle 11 (README:649-655) and the CLI reference (README:188) promise S1 is skippable via --user-profile and 'skipped by default in autonomous mode' (README:88). In code, --user-profile is parsed (cli.py:85) but never read anywhere — grep over cli.py/pipeline.py shows args.user_profile is never referenced, and s1_assess.run() has no profile-injection path. So S1 always runs. In headless mode (use_web_ipc = not sys.stdin.isatty(), s1_assess.py:685), each question blocks on a 300s file-poll timeout (_WEB_TIMEOUT, s1_assess.py:38, 369-403); a cron/CI/batch run stalls ~40-75 minutes and then synthesizes a profile from empty answers. Similarly S3's web review blocks 600s then SILENTLY defaults to lumper (s3_graph.py:54, 78-101) — README:388 instead claims the pipeline 'emits pipeline_paused and exits cleanly', which it never does. For a product run concurrently by many users, the human gates must be an async pause/persist/notify/resume job model, not in-process polling that fabricates defaults on timeout.

issues.title: No cross-run caching and no cross-process rate-limit coordination — external API layer cannot scale past one run per host
issues.detail: All external data (Wikipedia, PyPI, arXiv, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar) is cached only inside a run's state dir (e.g. audit/sources/sources_{domain_id}.json, s4_audit.py:226-258); re-running the same paper refetches everything. README:869 claims DiskCache ('SQLite-backed for deterministic API calls') is part of the stack — it is not in pyproject.toml dependencies and is never imported. Rate limiters are module-level globals (_ss_limiter in bibliography.py:65-90, _OPENALEX_LIMITER in sources.py:40-47) scoped to one process; each pipeline run is a separate subprocess (spawned by observe.py), so N concurrent runs each get their own 'serialized' limiter and collectively send N× the per-IP budget to Semantic Scholar — guaranteed 429 cascades exactly when concurrency matters. SS unauthenticated limits are per-IP, so a multi-tenant deployment shares one budget across all users with no queue, broker, or shared cache to mediate it. This is the binding throughput ceiling for the SaaS goal, and nothing in the architecture addresses it.

issues.title: SS rate limit configured for an authenticated key but never conditioned on key presence
issues.detail: config.yaml:21-23 sets semantic_scholar max_rate 1/time_period 1 with the comment 'authenticated key: 1 req/sec'. _get_ss_limiter (bibliography.py:77-90) reads this unconditionally; nothing checks whether SS_API_KEY is actually set (it is optional per README:305). Unauthenticated SS allows roughly 100 req/5 min (~0.33 req/s; CLAUDE.md says 0.1 req/s) — so the default configuration overruns the unauthenticated limit 3-10×, and the elaborate cooldown circuit breaker (_ss_cooldown_until, 30s→120s backoff) exists largely to absorb a self-inflicted overrun. Additionally _SS_API_KEY is read once at module import (bibliography.py:62), so a key injected later (e.g. via the web UI session env) inside the same process is ignored. The limiter should derive its rate from key presence and re-read the key per request.

issues.title: S4 adversarial gap loop is a stateless re-roll: rounds share no memory, termination condition can essentially never fire, last round wins
issues.detail: _run_gap_loop (s4_audit.py:91-198) runs finder→defender→rebuttal up to 3 rounds, but each round's _GAP_FINDER_PROMPT is byte-identical (only domain/terms/anchors — no prior verdicts, no prior gaps). The stall check compares set equality of free-text gap_description strings across independent LLM generations (s4_audit.py:176-185), which will almost never match — so the loop runs max rounds (9 LLM calls/domain at deep) and then returns only the LAST round's rebuttal_result, discarding rounds 1-2 entirely. The extra rounds add cost without information gain. README:636 also claims 'Every round is persisted to disk before scoring — a crash at round 2 of 3 restarts from round 1' — no round artifacts are written anywhere in s4_audit.py; gap results exist only in memory until gap_analysis.md is written at stage end.

issues.title: Phantom CLI/feature surface: six advertised flags do nothing; README documents subsystems that don't exist
issues.detail: Parsed but never used: --user-profile (cli.py:85), --stage (cli.py:84), --no-bibliography-fetch (cli.py:87, zero other references — README:190 advertises 'air-gapped mode'), --no-pdf (cli.py:76, never forwarded to run_pipeline at cli.py:165-175 whose no_pdf defaults False), --human (cli.py:75). --resume is forwarded to resume_stage (pipeline.py:110) which is never read — resume works only via stage_is_complete markers, so '--resume 4' is a no-op token. --renderer typst (README:182, 857) does not exist in cli.py at all. README further claims a Crossref tier (README:137, 525, 848 — 'crossref' appears nowhere in know_expand/), DiskCache, and map_a/map_b dual map outputs (README:954-957 — S2 writes a single map_{chunk_id}.json, s2_extract.py:62). For a product, every one of these is a user-facing lie; the README is a roadmap masquerading as documentation and needs a hard reconciliation pass before any external user touches it.

issues.title: URL ingestion writes raw HTML straight into the pipeline; no content extraction, content-type check, size cap, or SSRF guard
issues.detail: s0_ingest.py:49-69: for http(s) inputs, resp.text (raw HTML including <script>, nav, boilerplate) is written to source.txt and word-split into 800-word chunks; spaCy noun-chunks the first 50k chars of markup as 'structural zones'. Every downstream stage (term extraction, interview concepts, taxonomy) then operates on tag soup. There is no content-type check (a URL to a PDF is decoded as text), no readability/Docling pass, no response size limit (memory exhaustion on large responses), no User-Agent (many sites 403), and — because the web UI accepts arbitrary URLs to start runs — an SSRF vector against internal networks in any hosted deployment. README:316 lists URL as a first-class input; in practice this path produces garbage for typical web pages.

issues.title: S2 LLM signal silently sees only ~37% of each chunk
issues.detail: Chunks are built with max_tokens=4000 (config.yaml:53, cl100k ≈ 16k chars for dense prose), but the Signal-B map prompt truncates to text[:cfg.chunking.llm_map_char_limit] = 6,000 chars (s2_extract.py:93, config.yaml:55). The conceptual-extraction signal — the only one that captures implicit domain concepts — is blind to roughly the latter 60% of every chunk, with no event or warning. This directly violates the project's own design principle 1 ('bounded execution… guarantees silent omission' README:578-582): the bound exists, but it silently truncates instead of sub-chunking. Either lower chunk max_tokens or split chunks for the map call.

issues.title: Document's own references are extracted then thrown away; bibliography is built from generic domain-label keyword searches instead
issues.detail: S0 extracts the source PDF's reference strings to source_refs_raw.json (s0_ingest.py:80-88) and bibliography.py implements fetch_source_refs (line 319) to resolve them via SS — but it has zero callers (grep confirms only the definition). S4 even emits a 'source_refs_skipped / not_pdf' event for non-PDFs (s4_audit.py:378-383) implying PDFs use them; they never do. Instead, anchors and both bibliography buckets are fetched by searching SS with the bare domain LABEL (e.g. 'machine learning') sorted by citationCount (bibliography.py:285-310, 357-411), which returns field-generic mega-cited classics with no connection to the specific document. The single most relevant, already-in-hand citation pool — the paper's own bibliography — is discarded, while the gap analysis 'diffs' the graph against generic field papers. This undercuts design principle 4 (grounded citations) at its root: the pool is real but largely irrelevant.

issues.title: S3 Phase 2 silently descoped: 'two-agent classification' is a keyword-overlap heuristic and classification_conflicts.json is always empty
issues.detail: README:394-396 and the state-layout docs describe two agents classifying terms against the locked taxonomy with divergences flowing to S4 as 'primary gap candidates'. In code, _classify_term (s3_graph.py:352-375) is pure keyword/token overlap; _CLASSIFIER_PROMPT (s3_graph.py:199-207) is dead text; conflicts is initialized to [] at s3_graph.py:378 and never appended, so classification_conflicts.json is always empty and S4's gap_candidates derivation (s4_audit.py:391-396, 419-423) is vacuous code. Worse, terms with zero keyword overlap are assigned to the currently least-populated domain (s3_graph.py:371-375) — arbitrary placement that quietly pollutes domains and downstream per-domain research. Either implement the documented LLM classification or document the heuristic and route no-match terms to an 'unassigned' bucket.

issues.title: The 'non-negotiable' 65/35 split is a config knob applied to the wrong variable
issues.detail: The split is declared non-negotiable in CLAUDE.md and README:1019 yet lives in config.yaml:2 (foundational_fraction: 0.65) where any user can change it — the invariant is rhetorical, not enforced. More substantively: the ratio governs how many results are kept from two keyword searches whose relevance is the real quality bottleneck (see bibliography finding above), so tuning the ratio is second-order. A fixed ratio across all fields also ignores publication velocity — a 24-month frontier window for ML and for pure mathematics yield wildly different signal density (and _FIELD_BASELINES in bibliography.py:16-40 stops at 2023/2024, so in 2026 nearly all frontier papers fall through to the recency-factor fallback, making the MNCS machinery mostly dead weight). Defensible position: hard-code the EXISTENCE of the frontier bucket (README:677 already says this), make the ratio per-domain adaptive or at least honestly configurable, and delete or update the stale baselines table.

issues.title: Boilerplate filter uses substring matching and kills legitimate domain terms
issues.detail: compute_centrality rejects any term where any boilerplate token is a SUBSTRING of the name: `any(bp in name for bp in BOILERPLATE)` (centrality.py:21). 'zero-knowledge proof', 'proof assistant', 'hash table', 'lookup table', 'cross-section', 'figure of merit' are all silently dropped (return None → term never enters terms.json, s2_extract.py:450-451). For math/crypto/systems documents this deletes core vocabulary. Should be exact match or word-boundary match on the full term.

issues.title: Systematic occurrence-count inflation in the S2 reduce phase
issues.detail: TermOccurrence.occurrence_count defaults to 1 (schemas.py:15). The reduce aggregation creates a fresh TermOccurrence and then ADDS every observed count (s2_extract.py:414-419: created with implicit count=1, then += t.occurrence_count including the first occurrence) → +1 per unique term. The alias-cluster merge repeats the pattern (s2_extract.py:436-441) → another +1 per cluster plus +1 per absorbed member. Net: every singleton term's count is inflated by +2, clusters by more. With core_effective_threshold=10 and supporting_effective_threshold=4 (config.yaml:13-18), this systematically promotes borderline noise into supporting/core tiers. Initialize with occurrence_count=0 or copy the first record's count.

issues.title: S3 violates the codebase's own documented anti-pattern: taxonomy force-approved after editor exit; OpenAlex validation blocks the event loop
issues.detail: Two issues in s3_graph.py: (1) The edit path re-reads taxonomy.json after the editor closes and then unconditionally sets data['status'] = 'approved' (s3_graph.py:147-150) — the exact anti-pattern README:935 calls out ('the user may have quit without saving... verify status: approved before proceeding'). A user who quits vi without saving gets the pristine lumper proposal approved under mode 'edited'. (2) _validate_openalex uses synchronous httpx.get inside the async stage (s3_graph.py:240-253) and is called in a serial loop over up to 16 domains × 10s timeout (s3_graph.py:301-307), blocking the event loop (and the event/emit heartbeat the dashboard polls) for up to ~2.5 minutes. Also note OpenAlex /concepts is deprecated (frozen) in favor of /topics — validation quality will decay.

issues.title: S4 resume re-pays the full gap loop for already-completed domains
issues.detail: When the bibliography sentinel exists (bib_path non-empty, s4_audit.py:263-275), _process_domain skips the fetches but UNCONDITIONALLY re-runs the entire 3-round gap loop (up to 9 LLM calls) for that domain. Gap results are never persisted per domain — only aggregated into gap_analysis.md after ALL domains finish (s4_audit.py:437-443). A crash at domain 7 of 8 therefore re-runs the gap loop for domains 1-6 on resume, contradicting the idempotency story (README:733-752, principle 10) and multiplying cost. Persist a gaps_{domain_id}.json sentinel alongside the bibliography and short-circuit on it.

issues.title: Interview 'coverage' is satisfied by question text alone — a fully unanswered interview completes silently with a fabricated profile
issues.detail: _detect_covered_fields scans the concatenation of question AND answer text for keywords (s1_assess.py:258-273), so merely ASKING about math comfort marks math_comfort covered even when the web answer timed out and returned '' (s1_assess.py:403). After ~8 unanswered questions all fields read as covered, the agent may declare completion, and _synthesize_profile then infers an entire UserProfile from a transcript of empty answers (s1_assess.py:546-566) — no warning event distinguishes 'user answered' from 'user absent' (stage1_headless_no_answer fires only in the TTY branch, s1_assess.py:505-506). Downstream, every stage calibrates depth/math mode to a hallucinated reader. Coverage should require non-empty answers, and an all-timeouts interview should fall back to _DEFAULT_PROFILE with an explicit event.

issues.title: Source-fetch relevance gates are loose; unvetted third-party text is injected into S5 prompts
issues.detail: The Wikipedia gate accepts a title whose first word merely shares a 4-character prefix with the term (sources.py:160-167), and all S2 terms are lowercased (s2_extract.py:411), so acronym homonyms slip through ('cnn' → the news network; 'bert' → Sesame Street is blocked only if the extract doesn't contain 'bert', which it does). PyPI descriptions (arbitrary package READMEs, sources.py:188-227) and Wikipedia extracts are concatenated into S5 persona prompts with no sanitization — a prompt-injection surface once inputs come from untrusted users. The _is_searchable_term camelCase rejection (sources.py:99) is dead code since all terms are already lowercase by S4.

issues.title: Event names use stale stage numbering, fragmenting observability
issues.detail: S2 emits stage1_* events (s2_extract.py:288, 387-388, 406 — 'stage1_map_start', 's1_concept_grounding_*'), S3 emits stage2_* (s3_graph.py:287, 335), S4 emits stage3_* and s3_* (s4_audit.py:183, 188, 402) while their stage_start/stage_complete events carry the NEW numeric stage ids (2, 3, 4). Any dashboard or log consumer keying on event names misattributes events to the wrong stage. A mechanical rename plus a naming convention test would close this.

production_gaps: No multi-tenant story: per-run subprocess + file-polling IPC (qa_queue.jsonl, taxonomy_choice.json) + module-global rate limiters means concurrent users on one host multiply Semantic Scholar request rates per shared IP with no broker, queue, or shared cache. A shared HTTP cache (the DiskCache the README already claims) plus a single rate-limit-aware fetch service is the minimum before two users can run simultaneously.

No input hardening for hosted use: URL fetch has no SSRF protection, content-type check, size cap, or User-Agent (s0_ingest.py:26-31); Docling parse has no timeout, page cap, or memory bound — a large or adversarial PDF upload is a denial-of-service vector.
No OCR path: scan-only PDFs are rejected with an error (correctly), but partially scanned PDFs pass the guard (structural_zones>=5 OR chunks>=3) and silently lose all image-page content.

Human checkpoints (S1 interview, S3 taxonomy) need an async pause/exit/notify/resume job model. Current in-process polling with 300s/600s timeouts silently fabricates defaults (empty-answer profile, lumper taxonomy) — acceptable for a personal tool, indefensible for paying users.

S2→S4 wall-clock at unauthenticated SS rates: per-academic-core-term grounding searches (s2_extract.py:287-319) + ~6-8 SS calls per domain in S4 put a single run at tens of minutes of pure rate-limit waiting without SS_API_KEY; there is no batching (SS supports batch endpoints) and no cross-run reuse of identical queries.

Zero test coverage for S0 ingestion, the S1 interview state machine, and the S2 reduce pipeline (tests/ covers centrality, sources, bibliography, union_find only) — the three stages with the most environment-dependent failure modes ship untested.

README/CLI reconciliation: six no-op flags, a nonexistent --renderer, and documented-but-absent subsystems (Crossref tier, DiskCache, map_a/map_b artifacts, per-round critique persistence, pipeline_paused exit) must be either implemented or deleted from docs before external users arrive.
strengths: S0's degenerate-parse guard (s0_ingest.py:97-103) fails fast on scan-only PDFs with an actionable message instead of letting downstream stages silently degrade — exactly the right failure mode.

S2's three-signal design is genuinely complementary (deterministic spaCy, geometric KeyBERT/BGE-M3, conceptual LLM), with code-stripping before NLP signals, per-chunk .done map caching for cheap resume, and a thoughtful term-cleaning gauntlet (box-drawing rejection, JSON-fragment rejection, article+noun filtering).

The Semantic Scholar client is carefully engineered for a single process: 1-token serialized limiter, global 429 cooldown circuit breaker shared across coroutines, capped exponential backoff, DOI dedup, anchor-neighbor frontier expansion, and rich ss_* telemetry events for every request.
SS grounding demotion in S2 (academic core terms with zero SS hits demoted to supporting, s2_extract.py:321-342) is a cheap, effective hallucination guard on the term inventory.

sources.py is uniformly best-effort with exception containment, term-type-routed source selection, a relevance gate that catches the worst disambiguation mismatches, and a PyPI stub filter — failures degrade prompts, never crash the run.

The interview implementation anticipates real LLM misbehavior: embedded-option extraction from question text, hardcoded fallback options for the structured turns, coverage-override loop preventing premature completion, and dual TTY/web delivery.
code.summary: The S0-S4 subsystem is a well-instrumented single-user research tool with genuinely good ideas (3-signal extraction, two-bucket bibliography, term-type-routed source fetching, SS circuit breaker), but it is nowhere near the production-grade multi-user product the README describes. The gap between stated intent and code is the dominant problem: six advertised CLI flags are no-ops (including --user-profile, the only documented way to skip the mandatory human interview), the documented Crossref/DiskCache/two-agent-classification/round-persistence features do not exist, and the document's own reference list — extracted in S0 — is silently discarded while bibliographies are built from generic domain-label keyword searches. Concurrency is the structural ceiling: per-process module-global rate limiters, no cross-run caching, file-polling human checkpoints that silently fabricate defaults on timeout, and an SS limiter configured for an authenticated key regardless of whether one exists. Within stages, several quiet correctness bugs (LLM map signal truncated to ~37% of each chunk, substring boilerplate filter killing terms like 'zero-knowledge proof', systematic +2 occurrence inflation, a stateless 'adversarial' loop that always runs max rounds and keeps only the last roll) erode exactly the extraction and audit quality the architecture exists to guarantee.

verdicts.title: Mandatory human interview (S1) with broken bypass makes the default pipeline human-gated — incompatible with unattended/multi-user operation
verdicts.reasoning: Every cited code fact verifies. (1) cli.py:85 parses --user-profile but args.user_profile is never read; run_pipeline() (pipeline.py:101-110) has no profile parameter and s1_assess.run() (s1_assess.py:674-741) only skips via the pipeline.json stage marker — there is no profile-injection path. _DEFAULT_PROFILE (s1_assess.py:40) is dead code, never referenced. README:188, README:~88, and design principle 11 (README:649-655) all promise an S1 bypass that does not exist. (2) Headless mode confirmed: use_web_ipc = not sys.stdin.isatty() (s1_assess.py:685); _ask_web (s1_assess.py:369-403) blocks up to _WEB_TIMEOUT=300s per question and returns "" on timeout; the coverage-override loop (455-472) forces ~10-15 turns, so an unattended run stalls ~50-75 min then LLM-synthesizes a profile from empty answers (line 731) and marks the stage complete. (3) S3 confirmed: _prompt_taxonomy routes to web IPC when no TTY (s3_graph.py:119-120), polls 600s (_TAXONOMY_WEB_TIMEOUT, line 54), and on timeout defaults to lumper (line 100). No code emits pipeline_paused (state.py only has display formatting for that event name), so README:388's "emits pipeline_paused and exits cleanly" is false. Mitigations searched: --auto-taxonomy works for S3 (claim doesn't dispute), but no working S1 bypass exists anywhere (web UI /api/run passes no profile; no tests cover --user-profile). Trivial nuances only: the S3 timeout emits stage3_review_complete (mode=lumper) so it is "silent" only in that a timeout is indistinguishable from an explicit choice, and the stall floor is ~50 min rather than 40. Severity is not inflated for the objective layer: the README itself advertises autonomous/unattended operation, and the advertised bypasses are broken or fictional.

verdicts.title: No cross-run caching and no cross-process rate-limit coordination — external API layer cannot scale past one run per host
verdicts.reasoning: Every code-level observation checks out: (1) _ss_limiter (bibliography.py:65-90) and _OPENALEX_LIMITER (sources.py:40-47) are module-level aiolimiter globals with zero cross-process coordination — no fcntl/filelock/redis anywhere in the repo; (2) external-source results are cached only per-run at audit/sources/sources_{domain_id}.json (s4_audit.py:226-258), and _spawn_pipeline (observe.py:2445) mints a fresh run_id per non-resume run, so re-running the same paper refetches all Wikipedia/PyPI/arXiv/OpenAlex/SS data; (3) README:869 lists DiskCache in the present-tense stack table (and README:884 rejects Redis because "DiskCache is sufficient"), yet diskcache is absent from pyproject.toml dependencies and never imported — a genuine doc/code mismatch; (4) the POST /api/run handler (observe.py:2688) spawns a pipeline subprocess without checking pipeline_running, so N concurrent runs with independent per-process SS limiters are mechanically possible and would collectively exceed the per-IP budget. However, the framing and severity are inflated. The "SaaS goal" the claim calls this a binding ceiling for does not exist: grep for saas/tenant/multi-user across all .md/.py/.yaml files returns zero hits, and the README's "What not to use" table explicitly rejects Redis/Ray/Celery as distributed overkill — single-host, single-run scope is a documented deliberate design choice. "Guaranteed 429 cascades" is also overstated: bibliography.py:145-200 implements a Retry-After-honoring circuit breaker (_ss_cooldown_until) that pauses all SS tasks in a process on 429, so concurrent runs degrade to retry-paced throughput rather than uncontrolled cascade. For the project as actually scoped (local single-user CLI with one active run in the web UI), per-run caching and per-process limiters are adequate; the real defects are a README documentation bug (DiskCache), wasteful refetching across re-runs of the same input, and a missing concurrent-spawn guard in /api/run — real issues, but not architecture-critical for any goal the repo states.
verdicts.correction: The mechanics are all true (per-process limiters, per-run-only caching, DiskCache documented at README:869 but never implemented, unguarded /api/run concurrent spawning), but the severity is wrong. There is no SaaS or multi-tenant goal anywhere in the repo — the README explicitly scopes the project to single-host local use and rejects distributed infrastructure by design, so "binding throughput ceiling for the SaaS goal" judges the architecture against a requirement it never claims. Additionally, "guaranteed 429 cascades" overstates the failure mode: a per-process circuit breaker (bibliography.py:145-200) honors Retry-After and pauses all SS tasks on 429, so concurrent runs degrade gracefully rather than cascading. Accurate severity: a minor documentation bug (DiskCache), a moderate efficiency gap (refetch on re-run), and a missing single-run guard in the web API — not a critical architecture flaw.

verdicts.title: SS rate limit configured for an authenticated key but never conditioned on key presence
verdicts.reasoning: The core claim is materially correct and verified against the code. (1) /Users/cyan/ccr/know-expand/config.yaml lines 20-23 set semantic_scholar max_rate=1/time_period=1 with the literal comment "authenticated key: 1 req/sec". (2) _get_ss_limiter at /Users/cyan/ccr/know-expand/know_expand/bibliography.py:77-90 consumes this unconditionally; a repo-wide grep confirms no code anywhere conditions the rate on SS_API_KEY presence — the key (bibliography.py:62, read at module import) is used only for the optional x-api-key header at lines 150 and 223. (3) README.md:305 and CLAUDE.md:147 document the key as optional and the unauthenticated rate as 0.1 req/s, so the default keyless config overruns the project's own documented unauth limit 10x. (4) The 429 circuit breaker (bibliography.py:145-208, 30s→120s doubling backoff, global _ss_cooldown_until, 5 retries) exists as described and is what absorbs the resulting 429s; worse than the claim states, after retry exhaustion line 209 calls resp.raise_for_status() on the final 429, so the overrun can raise into a stage, not just slow it down. Severity "high" is defensible for default keyless runs. However, the "Additionally" sub-claim is refuted: the "key injected later via the web UI session env inside the same process" scenario cannot occur. observe.py has no key-setting endpoint (GET /api/keys only reads bool(os.environ.get(...)); there is no os.environ[...]= write anywhere in the file), and the pipeline always runs as a fresh subprocess (observe.py:2521-2528, env=os.environ.copy()) in which cli.py calls load_dotenv() (cli.py:7-8) before bibliography.py is imported (pipeline import deferred to cli.py:164). So the import-time read picks up the key correctly in every real execution path; it is a latent code-smell, not a live bug.
verdicts.correction: The rate-limit half of the claim is fully correct: the 1 req/s SS limiter is never conditioned on SS_API_KEY presence and overruns the documented unauthenticated limit (0.1 req/s per the repo's own README/CLAUDE.md) by 10x by default, with the 30s-120s cooldown breaker absorbing the self-inflicted 429s — and after 5 failed retries bibliography.py:209 raise_for_status() actually raises, so impact can exceed mere slowdown. The stale-key half is wrong in practice: there is no web UI mechanism that injects SS_API_KEY into a running process (observe.py's /api/keys is read-only and never writes os.environ), and the pipeline is always a freshly spawned subprocess that runs load_dotenv() before bibliography.py is imported, so the module-import-time read of _SS_API_KEY picks up the key in every actual execution path. The recommended fix should be limited to deriving the limiter rate from key presence; per-request key re-reading addresses a scenario that does not exist in this architecture.

verdicts.title: S4 adversarial gap loop is a stateless re-roll: rounds share no memory, termination condition can essentially never fire, last round wins
verdicts.reasoning: Every material sub-claim checks out against the code. (1) Stateless rounds: in _run_gap_loop (know_expand/stages/s4_audit.py:91-198), terms_str and anchor_str are computed once before the loop (lines 99-100) and the _GAP_FINDER_PROMPT format args (lines 112-117) are all loop-invariant — no prior gaps, defender arguments, or verdicts are injected, so each round's finder prompt is byte-identical. (2) Dead stall check: line 176 builds the gap-ID set from free-text gap_description strings and line 181 requires exact set equality across independent LLM generations; the router call path (agents/base.py call → _do_call_with_thinking) sets no temperature, so exact-match across independent samples is vanishingly unlikely. (3) Max cost: config.yaml adversarial_rounds.deep=3, 3 calls/round = 9 LLM calls/domain at deep. (4) Last round wins: rebuttal_result is overwritten each iteration and only the final one is returned (line 198); rounds 1-2 are discarded, so extra rounds add cost with no information gain. (5) README:636 ("Every round is persisted to disk before scoring") and README:850 ("round files prevent crash rework" for S4/S5) are false for S4: s4_audit.py writes only the sources cache, anchors, bibliography, and the stage-end gap_analysis.md/corrections.md — no per-round artifacts (repo grep confirms round files exist only in s5_research.py:845). The resume path (s4_audit.py:262-275) even re-runs the full gap loop when the bibliography sentinel exists, confirming gap results are never persisted per-domain. No mitigating code found anywhere; emit() events carry counts only and are not read for resume. One minor overbreadth: the title says "termination condition can essentially never fire," but a second exit (no_gaps, lines 127-131/178-180) can fire if the rebuttal dismisses all gaps — however the claim body correctly scopes the dead-code argument to the stall check, and when real gaps persist the loop does run to max rounds. Severity "high" is defensible for an architecture finding: ~48 wasted calls per 8-domain deep run, non-functional convergence logic, final output determined by a single uncorrelated round, and documentation misstating crash-safety.
verdicts.correction: Only a minor title-level overbreadth: the loop has a second termination condition (no_gaps — finder returns zero gaps, or rebuttal marks all gaps not_a_gap/ambiguous) that can genuinely fire; it is only the stall check (s4_audit.py:176-185) that is effectively dead code, exactly as the claim body states.

verdicts.title: URL ingestion writes raw HTML straight into the pipeline; no content extraction, content-type check, size cap, or SSRF guard
verdicts.reasoning: Every checkable sub-claim is accurate. (1) s0_ingest.py:26-31 `_fetch_url` returns raw `resp.text` with no User-Agent, no content-type check, and no size cap; httpx buffers the full body. (2) Lines 49-69: raw HTML is written to source.txt, word-split into 800-word chunks (config.yaml word_size: 800), and spaCy noun-chunks the first 50,000 chars of markup (config.yaml spacy_char_limit: 50000) into structural_zones. Docling is only used for local .pdf files; the URL branch gets no content extraction, and no readability/BeautifulSoup/trafilatura/html2text exists anywhere in the package or pyproject.toml. (3) A PDF URL is charset-decoded as text (mojibake) since resp.text is used unconditionally. (4) observe.py _spawn_pipeline (line 2445) passes the web UI's `input` param unvalidated to the CLI subprocess — no scheme allowlist or private-IP blocking, so the SSRF mechanism exists exactly as described. (5) README's S0 section (~line 316) does list URL as a first-class input. The repo even documents in sources.py:24 that missing User-Agent causes Wikipedia 403s, yet s0 sends none. Downstream stages (S2 extraction reads chunks; interview uses extracted terms) therefore operate on tag soup by construction. Severity 'high' is defensible for the execution-quality core.
verdicts.correction: One nuance: observe.py:2763 binds the dashboard to 127.0.0.1 only, so the SSRF vector is not exposed in the default configuration — it requires a deliberately hosted/proxied deployment, which the claim itself conditions on ("in any hosted deployment"). The POST /api/run endpoint also lacks CSRF protection, so the localhost bind is not a complete mitigation. This caps the default-config security blast radius but does not refute any stated fact.

verdicts.title: S2 LLM signal silently sees only ~37% of each chunk
verdicts.reasoning: The cited code is real but the quantified execution impact rests on an unreachable code path. CONFIRMED: (1) /Users/cyan/ccr/know-expand/know_expand/stages/s2_extract.py:93 slices the Signal-B map input to text[:cfg.chunking.llm_map_char_limit] with no truncation event or warning (chunk_map_start emits text_len but no truncation flag); (2) config.yaml:53-55 sets max_tokens: 4000 and llm_map_char_limit: 6000; (3) Signals A (spaCy, line 72) and C (KeyBERT, line 84) run on the full code-stripped chunk text — only the LLM signal is truncated, and its prompt is indeed the only one asked for implicit concepts ("Go beyond literal text"); (4) README design principle 1 says exactly what is quoted. REFUTED: the premise that chunks actually reach ~16k chars. The only path that uses max_tokens=4000 is the PDF branch (s0_ingest.py:90-94), and it cannot execute: HybridChunker(tokenizer="cl100k_base", max_tokens=4000) deterministically raises OSError at construction — installed docling-core 2.77.0 routes string tokenizers through HuggingFaceTokenizer.from_pretrained/AutoTokenizer, and "cl100k_base" is not a HuggingFace model (verified by direct construction in the project venv and huggingface_hub.repo_exists('cl100k_base')==False with working network; tokenizer config unchanged since the earliest commits; zero test coverage of the chunker; no runs/ data exists). The reachable ingestion paths (URL and plain-text) chunk at word_size=800 words ≈ 4,600-5,500 chars of prose, below the 6,000-char limit, so truncation essentially never fires in any run that completes S0. Therefore "silently sees only ~37% of each chunk" / "blind to the latter 60% of every chunk" at LAYER execution / SEVERITY high is wrong today: it is a latent design hazard that activates only after the (separate, unreported) S0 tokenizer bug is fixed. The recommended remediation (sub-chunk or emit a truncation event) is still sound for the intended design.
verdicts.correction: s2_extract.py:93 does silently truncate the LLM map input to 6,000 chars, but no chunk that large is ever produced by the executable code: the PDF path that would create ~16k-char chunks crashes at S0 (HybridChunker cannot load tokenizer "cl100k_base" — docling-core 2.77.0 treats string tokenizers as HuggingFace model ids), and the working URL/plain-text paths chunk at 800 words (~4.6-5.5k chars), under the limit. The finding is a latent design-level hazard (plus a missing truncation event), not a high-severity execution bug affecting "every chunk"; the more urgent bug is the broken cl100k_base tokenizer wiring in s0_ingest.py:90-94 / config.yaml:49.

code.summary: S5–S10 is an ambitious generate→reconcile→criticize→patch→verify→assemble chain whose anti-hallucination architecture (bounded bibliography before writing) is genuinely sound, but whose quality machinery is largely theater: the critic reviews only ~8k chars of each chapter, the aligner sees only the first 8k chars, S8 "verification" is regex key-membership plus a contradicts-only abstract check whose results go to a report nobody consumes, and S10 strips all [NEEDS_CITATION]/[INFERRED] markers before the reader sees them. Two sequencing/wiring bugs (S7 reads a bibliography file that S10 writes; S6 injects citation keys it never persists) guarantee broken or ungrounded citations in the shipped PDF, directly contradicting the README's headline "verified citations" claim. No stage can fail the build on quality grounds — every stage marks itself complete unconditionally, including S5 when every domain fails.
strengths: Ground-before-write citation design: S5 personas receive a bounded real bibliography (s5_research.py:96-97, README.md:425) — the correct anti-hallucination architecture; fabricating a paper requires inventing a key that S8 will at least flag.
Per-domain sentinel files + atomic_write for sections/summaries (s5_research.py:663-680, 917-924) give crash-safe per-domain resume within S5.
Deterministic patch application — LLM plans, Python applies (s6_align.py:_apply_patch, s9_prereq.py) — is a sound pattern that avoids letting the model rewrite whole files.
Critic loop has real convergence engineering: bounded rounds per depth, Jaccard-based stall detection, persisted critique artifacts (s5_research.py:827-911).
S8 strips fenced/inline code before scanning and allowlists pipeline markers (s8_verify.py:24-32, 49-51), avoiding the obvious [@variable] false-positive class.
s10_assemble.py:_wrap_bare_math_in_segment is a careful brace-depth walker with word-boundary guards, and _sanitize_bib_entry correctly hardens CSL-JSON against citeproc null crashes.
Depth-aware prompt caps (config.yaml research_context) with documented measured sizes (44k→11k chars) show real cost/latency discipline in S5.

issues.title: Headline product claim 'verified citations / grounds every claim' is not what the system does
issues.detail: README.md:37-39 claims the product 'grounds every claim in verifiable, real citations' and ships 'verified citations'. What is actually verified: S8 marks a citation 'verified' iff its key exists in a bibliography JSON (s8_verify.py:72-75) — pure key membership, no check that the paper supports the claim. The semantic layer (s8_verify.py:107-167) only runs when an abstract exists, caps at 50 pairs/domain (line 139), and only surfaces relation=='contradicts' (line 158) — 'mentions' (paper does not support the claim) is silently dropped. Then S10 deletes every [NEEDS_CITATION]/[INFERRED]/[UNVALIDATED] marker before assembly (s10_assemble.py:333-362 _clean_section_text), so an unciteable claim is rendered indistinguishable from a cited one in the final PDF. All three hallucination paths (fabricated claim + irrelevant-but-real key; unciteable claim with stripped marker; invented key rendered as broken citeproc text) reach the reader. Either the claim must be weakened to 'citation keys are validated against a real bibliography' or the verification layer must be rebuilt.

issues.title: Verification is report-only with no feedback path, and runs before the last two content-mutating stages
issues.detail: S8's outputs (needs_citation.md, citation_index.json, CITATION_MISMATCH entries) are written to audit/ and never read by S9 or S10 — even a detected contradiction changes nothing in the document (s8_verify.py:292-298). Worse, the pipeline order is verify → prereq → assemble (pipeline.py:93-95): S9 inserts LLM-generated primer text after the audit, and S10's roadmap injection adds more unaudited LLM text (s10_assemble.py:455-499), so the audited document is not the shipped document. No stage in S5–S10 can fail the build on any quality signal; mark_stage_complete is unconditional in every stage. For a product, 'verify' must either gate, fix, or annotate the output — currently it does none.

issues.title: S7 synthesize reads state_dir/bibliography.json which is only written by S10 — synthesis always cites from an empty pool on fresh runs
issues.detail: s7_synthesize.py:308-315 loads state_dir/'bibliography.json' for citation grounding, but the only writer of that path is s10_assemble.py:422-423, which runs three stages later. On every fresh run bibliography_keys is '', while _STRUCTURAL_PROMPT/_SEMANTIC_PROMPT still instruct 'cite these IDs when you support a claim' against an empty list — inviting the model to invent keys. This directly violates the project's own core invariant ('bibliography is the only citation pool', README.md:425) for the entire synthesis chapter, which README.md:631 itself calls 'the most hallucination-prone output'. Fix is one line: merge audit/bibliography_*.json in S7 (the helper already exists as _merge_bibliographies in s10_assemble.py:98).

issues.title: S6 align injects citation keys that are never added to any bibliography — guaranteed broken citations in the PDF
issues.detail: _SYSTEM_PROMPT_PASS2 instructs the model to cite SS results 'in the form [@<author>_<year>_<word>]' (s6_align.py:82) and patches insert those keys into section files, but _persist_bibliography is a literal no-op pass (s6_align.py:227-231). The keys therefore exist in no bibliography_{domain}.json: S8 flags them unknown_key (report-only), and pandoc --citeproc in S10 renders them as bold 'key?' placeholders in the final PDF. The stage's stated purpose — 'resolve [NEEDS_CITATION] via Semantic Scholar search and bibliography append' (README.md:489) — is half-implemented in a way that actively damages output.

issues.title: Critic and aligner can only see a fraction of the chapter they are supposed to enforce quality on
issues.detail: _compact_narrative truncates the chapter to head 3000 + tail 5000 chars before the critic sees it (s5_research.py:518-530, used at 840), while _CRITIC_PROMPT demands checking 'EVERY' equation for symbol tables, worked examples, etc. (s5_research.py:301-317). A deep-depth chapter is tens of thousands of chars — the middle is never criticized in any round, so multi-round revision converges on a document whose bulk was never reviewed. Same pattern in S6: the aligner sees only the first 8000 chars (s6_align.py:264-266) yet returns whole-document checklist booleans and plans patches whose before:/after: anchors may lie in text it never saw; S9 has the identical 8k truncation (s9_prereq.py:115-118). Net effect: symbol tables, worked examples, intuition paragraphs, and section ordering are enforced ~0% deterministically and only prompted-for; the 'enforcement' stages physically cannot check most of the document.

issues.title: Three-persona design's value is structurally capped by the single-call Reconciler bottleneck; ~4-10x researcher-class cost with no measurement
issues.detail: Per domain: 3 persona calls + 1 reconciler + up to 3 critic + up to 3 full-rewrite revise calls = up to 10 researcher-role calls (s5_research.py:778-903). The reconciler must emit the ENTIRE merged chapter as one JSON string field in a single structured call (ReconcilerOutput.narrative, schemas.py:203-206) with no max_tokens set (_do_call, base.py:611-615) — output is bounded by one model call's completion limit regardless of how much the three personas produced, so most persona content is necessarily discarded. Each revise round regenerates the whole narrative (s5_research.py:894-903), re-paying full output cost and risking shrinkage with no length/regression guard. The personas do contribute distinct section templates, but the same coverage could come from one call with the combined outline at ~1/4 cost; there is no eval or ablation anywhere demonstrating the panel beats that baseline. Additionally, the S5/S7 critics use the expensive 'researcher' role (s5_research.py:966, s7_synthesize.py:304) while models.yaml defines a cheaper 'critic' role that only S4 uses — paying researcher prices for critique.

issues.title: Failed domains are unrecoverable: S5 marks the stage complete even when domains (or all domains) fail
issues.detail: s5_research.py:990-1016 gathers all domains with return_exceptions=True, logs failures, then unconditionally calls mark_stage_complete(state_dir, 5). Because stage_is_complete short-circuits the whole stage on resume (s5_research.py:949-951), a failed domain can never be retried through the normal resume path — its chapter is simply absent, S10 emits s7_section_missing and ships a PDF silently missing entire domains. In the worst case (quota exhaustion, all domains fail) the pipeline still 'succeeds' end-to-end: S7 writes a placeholder synthesis (s7_synthesize.py:289-300) and S10 produces a title-plus-bibliography PDF. For a paid product this is silent total failure reported as success. mark_stage_complete should be withheld (or a partial marker written) when failed > 0.

issues.title: README promises multiple S10/S8 safety mechanisms that do not exist in code
issues.detail: Documented but unimplemented: (1) '--renderer xelatex | typst' (README.md:181, 857) — no such flag in cli.py; (2) explicit 'xelatex pass 1 / pass 2 ... two passes are mandatory' (README.md:563-565, CLAUDE.md 'Two xelatex passes — always') — s10_assemble.py:574-580 makes a single pandoc invocation with no pass control and no TOC is even requested; (3) 'pypdf integrity check ... raise before checkpoint is written' (README.md:566, 670, 917) — _count_pdf_pages swallows every exception and returns None (s10_assemble.py:640-649); the only gate is st_size > 0 (line 598) and the stage marks complete even on pandoc failure (line 629); (4) 'Acceptance criterion: 0 [UNVERIFIED] tags' (README.md:530) — no code anywhere counts or gates on such tags; (5) 'round files prevent crash rework' (README.md:850, 636) — critique round files are written but never read back; a crash restarts the domain from the personas. Meanwhile the roadmap prioritizes --batch-mode cost optimization (CLAUDE.md) over closing the verification gap. The docs describe the product the code should be; users and contributors will plan against guarantees that aren't there.

issues.title: S5 bibliography expansion: missing-ID resolution is dead code and [NEEDS_CITATION] resolution is unverified citation attachment
issues.detail: _title_relevance (s5_research.py:364-369) computes word overlap of query tokens vs title tokens. For missing citation IDs the query is the ID itself (e.g. 'vaswani_2017_attention'), a single token that can never appear in a title word set, so relevance is always 0 and the >=0.4 gate (line 453) never passes — the missing-ID branch (lines 447-456) is a guaranteed no-op that still burns one SS API call per hallucinated key. The [NEEDS_CITATION] branch (lines 462-479) replaces the marker with [@id] purely on sentence-vs-title word overlap — no abstract check, no LLM check — converting an honestly-flagged unciteable claim into a 'cited' one (citation laundering); and because a long sentence needs 40% of its tokens to appear in a ~10-word title, it almost never fires, so in practice the advertised 'A-3 bibliography expansion' does close to nothing while emitting success events. The bib write at line 502 is also non-atomic (plain write_text) unlike every other artifact.

issues.title: Final PDF gets two bibliographies and broken multi-citation handling
issues.detail: S10 appends a hand-rolled '## Bibliography' markdown section (s10_assemble.py:507, _bibliography_to_markdown:155-188) AND runs pandoc with --citeproc (line 578), which appends its own citeproc-generated references section — the shipped PDF contains two differently-formatted bibliographies. Separately, S8's key regex \[@?([\w\-]{3,})\] (s8_verify.py:24) cannot match pandoc multi-citation syntax [@a; @b] (which _convert_cite_syntax in s10_assemble.py:342-344 itself produces), so multi-cites are never audited; and bracketed years/words like [2017] or [GitHub] are reported as unknown_key false positives (the islower() guard at s8_verify.py:69 only filters lowercase).

issues.title: LaTeX math fixers interact incoherently: _fix_bare_math re-injects $ into \[...\] blocks that _fix_mixed_display_math just cleaned
issues.detail: _clean_section_text runs _fix_mixed_display_math (strips lone $ inside \[...\], s10_assemble.py:309-330) BEFORE _fix_bare_math (s10_assemble.py:361). But _fix_bare_math's segment splitter (line 295) only recognizes `...`, $...$ and $$...$$ as existing math — not \[...\] or \(...\) — so any \frac, \sum, Greek letter etc. inside a \[...\] display block gets wrapped in $...$, recreating exactly the invalid nesting the previous pass removed. Since pandoc markdown treats \[ as an escaped literal bracket, these blocks degrade to stray brackets around inline-math fragments in the PDF. The fixer also rewrites prose: any backslash-command lookalike outside a code fence (e.g. a file path or shell text in plain prose) is force-wrapped in math mode. This whole layer is heuristic patching of unconstrained LLM output with no validation pass (no pandoc dry-run, no latex lint) before the 300s single-shot build (line 587).

issues.title: Prompt-cache engineering is inert in the default configuration
issues.detail: The cache_control ephemeral shared block (s5_research.py:739-758) only does anything on Anthropic models, but models.yaml puts claude-opus-4-7/sonnet at positions 6-7 of the researcher chain behind geminicli (subprocess that flattens content blocks to plain text, base.py:52-56), gemini API, mistral and groq — so in the common path the block is dead weight. The in-code comment's claim that caching activates 'when parallel personas complete and the reconciler reuses the same prefix' (lines 735-738) is false twice over: the three personas fire simultaneously (cache write completes only after the first response) and the reconciler prompt (line 804) is a different single-string prompt that does not share the prefix. Real benefit is limited to retry/resume of the same persona call when an Anthropic model happens to be active. CLAUDE.md/README present this as a working cost optimization.

issues.title: Stage-renumbering left event names and behavior pointing at old stage numbers across S6-S10
issues.detail: S6 emits s4_5_domain_* events (s6_align.py:252-329), S7 emits s5_structural_start/s5_critique_round/s5_critic_loop_done (s7_synthesize.py:323-427), S9 emits s6_5_primer_inserted/s6_5_finish (s9_prereq.py:149, 218), and S10 emits s7_bibliography_merged/s7_section_missing/s7_pdf_* (s10_assemble.py:426, 443, 556-615) — while genuinely-S5 and S7 code also emit identically-prefixed s5_* events. Any dashboard, log query, or alert keyed on event prefixes misattributes work across four stages; test files carry the same stale numbering (tests/test_s4_research.py tests S5, test_s6_verify.py tests S8, test_s7_assemble.py tests S10). Mechanical fix, real observability cost for a multi-user product.

issues.title: S6/S9 failure handling marks failed work as done; S7 critic loop revises against stale input and duplicates insights
issues.detail: In S6, an LLM error or missing section file touches the sentinel anyway (s6_align.py:277-287, 259-261), permanently recording an unaligned section as aligned. In S7's critic loop, after a revise round only current_structural is replaced (s7_synthesize.py:424) while current_semantic stays the original draft, so subsequent critic rounds compare a merged revision against a stale draft; and on accept-after-revise the final draft is built from current_structural.insights + current_semantic.insights (lines 392-397) where the revised draft already merged semantic content — duplicating insights in the capstone chapter. Both loops also reference rnd after the for-loop (s7_synthesize.py:427, s5_research.py:910), a latent NameError if adversarial_rounds is ever configured to 0.

issues.title: S6-S9 are sequential per-section LLM loops while S5 is fully parallel — unbalanced wall-clock profile for a product
issues.detail: S5 launches all domains and personas concurrently (s5_research.py:973-990), but S6 aligns domains one at a time (s6_align.py:361-363 await in a for loop), S8 classifies up to 50 citation pairs per domain strictly serially (s8_verify.py:154-166 — with the classifier chain headed by a geminicli subprocess with a 600s timeout, worst case is hours), and S9 threads sections serially (s9_prereq.py:197-216). For an 8-domain deep run the post-research stages can dominate wall-clock for no reason — these are embarrassingly parallel and already have per-domain sentinels. This matters for the stated concurrent-users goal and for the planned overnight --batch-mode story.

issues.title: Assorted S10 robustness gaps: dead code, CWD-relative CSL path, tight pandoc timeout
issues.detail: _topo_sort_domains (s10_assemble.py:27-45) is dead code that builds an unused dict and returns input order with a misleading docstring — the real sort is _topo_sort_domains_with_nodes. The CSL stylesheet is resolved as Path('style')/... relative to the process CWD (line 530), silently dropping citation styling when the pipeline runs from another directory (the web UI spawns subprocesses). The single pandoc+xelatex run has a 300s timeout (line 587) — for the advertised 241-page reference output this is marginal, and a timeout produces no partial diagnostics. The roadmap if/else at lines 482-485 has identical branches.

production_gaps: No quality gate anywhere in S5-S10 can fail or block a build: every stage calls mark_stage_complete unconditionally, including total-failure paths (all domains failed, pandoc failed, alignment errored). A SaaS needs at minimum a machine-readable run verdict (complete/partial/failed) derived from s5_domain_failed, s7_section_missing, s7_pdf_error and S8 counts.

No per-run cost ceiling or budget enforcement despite README estimating $50-150/deep run; a runaway critic loop or quota-fallback to Opus has no kill switch. model_usage.jsonl is logged but never acted on.

Verification needs a real design: either S8 gates assembly (configurable threshold on unknown_keys/mismatches), or S10 renders unverified claims visibly (footnote/endnote) instead of stripping markers (s10_assemble.py:333-362). The current 'logged, never a build failure' policy plus marker-stripping is indefensible for the 'verified citations' positioning.
No retry path for partially-failed S5 runs short of manually clearing the stage in pipeline.json; per-domain sentinels exist but are unreachable once the stage marker is set.

Reconciler/revise calls have no max_tokens, no output-length validation, and no shrinkage guard — chapter length is silently bounded by provider defaults and can regress across critic rounds with no detection.
No PDF validation beyond size>0: the README-promised pypdf integrity gate, minimum page count, and xelatex-corruption detection are unimplemented; a font-error-corrupted PDF ships as success.
Event-name schema is unversioned and stale across four stages (s4_5_*, s5_* in S7, s6_5_*, s7_* in S10), so any monitoring built for concurrent users will misattribute stage progress.

No golden-output or quality regression test exists for the pedagogical protocols (symbol tables, worked examples) — they are enforced only by prompts and a critic that sees 8k of the chapter; a deterministic linter (equation without preceding table, section-order check) would be cheap and is absent.

verdicts.reasoning:
Every cited behavior checks out, and the situation is actually worse than claimed.

1. S8 outputs are write-only with respect to the pipeline. s8_verify.py:292-298 writes needs_citation.md (including CITATION_MISMATCH entries from the contradiction classifier) and citation_index.json to audit/, then unconditionally calls mark_stage_complete (line 300). A repo-wide grep shows the only runtime consumer of needs_citation.md is observe.py:2333-2346, which merely counts '[NEEDS_CITATION]' occurrences for a dashboard stat; citation_index.json is read only by tests (tests/test_s6_verify.py). S9 (s9_prereq.py:101-161) makes a fresh LLM call per section and writes primer blockquotes directly into sections/section_*.md AFTER S8 audited those files; S10 (s10_assemble.py:455-499) injects a Reading Roadmap from summaries/summary_synthesis.json — a file S8 never scans (S8 only audits sections/section_*.md, s8_verify.py:226-229). No quality gating anywhere in S5–S10: mark_stage_complete fires on every non-crash path (s5_research.py:1010, s6_align.py:355/372, s7_synthesize.py:299/463, s8_verify.py:300, s9_prereq.py:180/224, s10_assemble.py:629). No counter (mismatches, unknown keys, needs_citation totals) influences control flow.

So the exact claims S8 flagged as unverified are shipped with their flags erased — the reader cannot even see that verification failed. 'Verify' therefore neither gates, nor fixes, nor annotates; S10 actively removes the annotations.

Mitigation considered and rejected as a refutation: CLAUDE.md documents '[NEEDS_CITATION] is logged, never a build failure' as an intentional constraint, and S5/S6 have intra-stage citation-resolution passes (s5_research.py:404-497, S6 align). But those run BEFORE S8, so they are not a feedback path from verification, and documented intent does not change the architectural fact that the audited document is not the shipped document. Severity 'critical' is defensible for a product whose headline feature is research-grade, citation-audited output.

verdicts.title: S7 synthesize reads state_dir/bibliography.json which is only written by S10 — synthesis always cites from an empty pool on fresh runs
verdicts.reasoning:
I attempted to refute this and could not — every load-bearing element checks out.

1. Read path: /Users/cyan/ccr/know-expand/know_expand/stages/s7_synthesize.py:306-315 reads `state_dir / "bibliography.json"`; when absent, `bibliography_keys` stays `""` and is unconditionally formatted into _STRUCTURAL_PROMPT (line 334) and _SEMANTIC_PROMPT (line 343).

3. Stage order: pipeline.py:92-96 wires align → synthesize → verify → prereq → assemble. S10 runs three stages after S7, so on every fresh run the file does not exist when S7 executes. Fresh runs get a new `runs/{run_id}/state`, so no stale file can rescue it.

4. Prompt behavior is actually worse than claimed: besides "cite these IDs when you support a claim" over an empty list (s7_synthesize.py:45-46, 74-75), _STRUCTURAL_PROMPT line 52 REQUIRES "At least one bibliography citation supporting the feasibility" per insight — mandating citations from an empty pool.

S8 verify (s8_verify.py:209-243) builds valid IDs from the real `audit/bibliography_*.json` files and marks fabricated keys as `unknown_key`, but it only counts and logs them into a report markdown (_build_needs_citation_md); it never strips or rewrites sections, and per project invariant this is never a build failure. The S7 adversarial critic loop has no bibliography access to catch fabricated keys either. So detection exists downstream, correction does not — fabricated keys reach the assembled document.

6. The proposed fix is viable: `_merge_bibliographies(audit_dir)` is defined at s10_assemble.py:98 and reads only from audit_dir, which S4 fully populates before S7 runs.

Severity "high" is defensible: every fresh run is affected, and the capstone synthesis chapter — which README.md's critic table explicitly labels "the most hallucination-prone output" — either ships with zero grounded citations or with invented keys that are flagged but never removed.

One pedantic nuance that does not change the verdict: the README invariant "The bibliography is the only citation pool" is phrased about "Stage 5 agents" specifically, not S7. verdicts.title: S6 align injects citation keys that are never added to any bibliography — guaranteed broken citations in the PDF
verdicts.reasoning: Every load-bearing element of the claim checks out against the code. (1) s6_align.py:82 contains the exact instruction "Use citation keys in the form [@<author>_<year>_<word>]" in _SYSTEM_PROMPT_PASS2, and _align_domain applies the resulting patches to section files via _apply_patch with no key validation. (2) _persist_bibliography (s6_align.py:227-231) is a literal `pass` no-op — and the claim actually understates it: the function is never called anywhere, and the companion _make_citation_id helper is dead code too. The only minor hedge is "guaranteed" — breakage technically requires the LLM to emit a key for a newly-found paper — but since the prompt explicitly instructs that and no resolution path exists for any such key, this is not a material overstatement. verdicts.title: Critic and aligner can only see a fraction of the chapter they are supposed to enforce quality on
verdicts.reasoning: Every cited code location behaves exactly as claimed. (1) s5_research.py:518-530 `_compact_narrative` keeps head 3000 + tail 5000 chars for any narrative over 8000 chars, and is used at line 840 to build the critic prompt in every adversarial round; the middle of a long chapter is positionally excluded in all rounds, while _CRITIC_PROMPT (lines 285-321) instructs whole-document checks ("Check EVERY item", symbol tables for any equation, worked examples for any abstract concept). The reviser receives the full narrative (line 898), but since the critic never sees the middle, no issues there are ever reported for revision — the loop converges with the bulk unreviewed. (2) s6_align.py:263-266 truncates the section to the first 8000 chars, yet the prompt requires whole-document checklist booleans (lines 45-56) and patch positions; `_apply_patch` fuzzy-matches anchors against the full file the planner never saw, and the checklist is only emitted as an event (line 320), gating nothing. (3) s9_prereq.py:115-118 has the identical [:8000] truncation; primers cannot be positioned for terms first used past 8k. Severity "high" is defensible for a product whose core promise is pedagogical completeness, since the quality-enforcement stages are the only mechanism and are blind to most of any long chapter.
verdicts.correction: Two precision notes, neither material: (a) the S5 truncation is a documented intentional design tradeoff (the reviser gets full text; the critic deliberately gets a window), not an unnoticed bug — but the behavioral consequence claimed (middle never criticized in any round) is accurate; (b) in S6 the more precise failure mode is that patches cannot be planned FOR text beyond the first 8000 chars and fuzzy anchor matching against the full file can mis-resolve, rather than anchors literally lying in unseen text.
