issues.title: Dashboard is architected as a single-user localhost operator console, which is incompatible with the stated SaaS/self-hosted multi-user goal
issues.detail: Every structural decision in observe.py assumes exactly one operator on one machine watching one run: bind to 127.0.0.1 (line 2763), a single global 'active' run resolved by mtime, no authentication, no per-user state, and file-based IPC. README line 20/174 and CLAUDE.md frame `serve` as a personal localhost tool. None of the API endpoints carry a run_id or user identity. This is not a hardening gap that can be patched at the edges; the core data model (one global active state_dir for all clients) must be redesigned around per-run / per-tenant addressing before this can host concurrent users. The objective ('many users run concurrently') and the artifact's design premise are in direct conflict.

issues.title: Single global 'active state dir' makes concurrent runs/users structurally impossible
issues.detail: Both do_GET and do_POST compute `state_dir = _find_active_state_dir(runs_dir)` (lines 2615, 2679), and _find_active_state_dir (lines 2021-2040) returns the single most-recently-modified live run. No endpoint (/api/status, /api/events, /api/stage, /api/section, /api/qa, /api/stop) accepts a run_id, so the dashboard can only ever reflect one run and every client sees the same one. Two pipelines running at once collide on 'which is active' by mtime, so a second user's poll silently re-targets the first user's run — answers, stop commands, and stage-clears land on the wrong run. The UI has a 'run drawer' implying multi-run, but the backend cannot honor it. This must become run-scoped routing (e.g. /api/run/{id}/status) before multi-user is viable.

issues.title: Single-threaded http.server + 2s full-file polling does not scale to multiple clients
issues.detail: The server is plain `http.server.HTTPServer` (line 2763), not ThreadingHTTPServer — all requests are serialized. The client polls every 2s (line 1464) hitting /api/status and /api/events, and /api/events returns the ENTIRE events.jsonl every call (_load_events, line 2387). Worse, _load_state and several _load_stage_artifacts branches (S5/S6/S8/S9, e.g. lines 2226-2247, 2338-2348) each re-read and re-parse the whole events.jsonl on every poll. events.jsonl grows unbounded during a run, so per-poll cost is O(file size) and a long run plus a few open tabs will saturate the single thread; one slow handler (large events file or markdown render) blocks the QA poll for every client. The ETag short-circuit (line 2599) still builds the full payload before comparing, so it saves bandwidth but not the read/parse/serialize cost. This needs SSE/websocket push with incremental tailing and a concurrent server.

issues.title: ~2000-line HTML/CSS/JS embedded as a Python string in a 2768-line single file is unmaintainable
issues.detail: observe.py mixes the entire frontend (template `_PAGE`) and the HTTP server in one file, with CLAUDE.md encoding the brittle invariant 'Python code is always below the HTML template string'. The JS cannot be linted, type-checked, unit-tested, or bundled; there is no template engine, no escaping helper, and no separation of concerns. For a hosted product this should be a real frontend (or at least templated static assets) served by a framework, so the dashboard can be tested and the XSS sinks below can be addressed centrally.

issues.title: No authentication or CSRF protection on any endpoint, including destructive POSTs
issues.detail: There is no auth check anywhere in do_GET/do_POST. Anyone able to reach the port can spawn pipelines (/api/run, line 2688), kill process groups (/api/stop, line 2697), wipe stage markers (/api/stage/:id/clear, line 2720), inject interview answers, and enumerate/read the filesystem. The only safeguard is the 127.0.0.1 bind. There is also no CSRF defense: POSTs accept application/json with no token and no Origin/Referer validation, so any web page the operator visits can issue cross-origin POSTs to localhost:7842 (and DNS-rebinding defeats the localhost assumption entirely). For a hosted or even self-hosted-on-a-LAN deployment this is a full remote-control + RCE-adjacent surface (it can launch subprocesses and read arbitrary files). Auth (session/token), CSRF tokens, and Origin checks are mandatory before exposure.

issues.title: Arbitrary filesystem enumeration via /api/files?dir=
issues.detail: _list_files (lines 2414-2442) takes the `dir` query param, runs Path(dir).expanduser().resolve() with no allowlist/jail, and returns every entry's name, type, absolute path, and size. `/api/files?dir=/` or `?dir=/Users` discloses the entire directory tree of the host (I verified dir=/etc resolves to /private/etc and would list it). On a shared/hosted box this leaks other tenants' run directories, home dirs, and the layout an attacker needs to target the .md-read traversal below. Must be confined to runs_dir.

issues.title: Path traversal in /api/section reads arbitrary .md files outside the run dir
issues.detail: do_GET builds `path = state_dir/'sections'/f'section_{sid}.md'` where sid comes straight from the URL with only split('?') and strip('/') (lines 2636-2637). BaseHTTPRequestHandler does NOT normalize `..` in self.path, so a request like /api/section/../../../../Users/victim/secret resolves (verified) outside the run directory to read any file ending in .md anywhere the server user can read. The `section_` prefix only consumes one `..` level and the `.md` suffix is the only constraint — still an arbitrary-markdown-file read and a filesystem-structure oracle. Combined with /api/files this is a practical exfiltration path. sid must be validated against the sections dir with a realpath containment check.

issues.title: Stored XSS: unescaped term names and unsanitized markdown HTML rendered via innerHTML
issues.detail: Multiple innerHTML sinks render source/LLM-derived strings without escaping. Term names from the ingested document are injected raw: `<span class="term-chip">${t.name}...` (line 1129). The section view renders Python-Markdown output directly: `view.innerHTML = d.html` (line 1290), and _render_section (line 2400) calls markdown.markdown(...) with no sanitizer (python-markdown passes raw HTML/`<script>`/`onerror` through by default). Since the source document (PDF/URL/text) is attacker-controllable in a hosted product, a crafted document executes script in the dashboard origin — which, given there is no auth/CSRF, can then drive /api/run, /api/stop, and the file-read endpoints. Other innerHTML sites (domain labels, summary previews at lines 1150/1178/1221/1270) share the issue. Needs output escaping plus HTML sanitization (e.g. bleach) of rendered markdown.

issues.title: /api/run accepts an arbitrary input path with no validation, becoming a file-read-to-output primitive
issues.detail: do_POST /api/run passes the client-supplied `input` field straight into _spawn_pipeline (line 2689), which forwards it as the document path to the CLI (line 2497/2510) with no allowlist or sandbox. A user can point the pipeline at any file on the host (config, other tenants' docs, secrets) and the pipeline will ingest it and surface its content in viewable sections/PDF — an exfiltration channel on a shared host. There is also no per-user/run authorization tying the input to the requester. (Note: args are passed as a Popen list, not shell=True, so there is no shell-injection, but the arbitrary-path read remains.) Input paths must be confined to an uploads area per user.

issues.title: Documented 'set API keys via web UI' feature does not exist; key/tenant isolation is absent
issues.detail: README line 296 and CLAUDE.md both state keys can be 'Set in .env or via the web UI (session only — not persisted to disk).' There is no POST /api/keys; /api/keys is GET-only and returns booleans (lines 2659-2672). So the documented capability is missing (intent-vs-code mismatch). Separately, _spawn_pipeline passes env=os.environ.copy() (line 2526), so every spawned run inherits the single server process's keys — there is no per-user/per-run key scoping. If the web-UI key feature were added as documented, posting plaintext keys to an unauthenticated, CSRF-less, non-HTTPS localhost endpoint would itself be a vulnerability. The good news: the current /api/keys never returns key values, only presence booleans.

issues.title: PID-file process control is vulnerable to PID reuse and stale files
issues.detail: Process management hangs entirely on a `pipeline_pid` text file. /api/stop does os.killpg(os.getpgid(pid), SIGTERM) on a PID read from that file (line 2705); if the original process exited and the OS recycled the PID, this signals an unrelated process group. _pipeline_is_running uses os.kill(pid,0) (line 2015) with the same reuse false-positive, and a stale pid file (process died without unlink) makes _find_active_state_dir prefer a dead run as 'live'. There is no generation token / start-time cookie to disambiguate, and no reconciliation of orphaned pipelines on server restart. A production design needs a supervised process registry, not a bare PID file.

issues.title: No concurrency cap or queue on /api/run; unbounded heavy subprocess spawning
issues.detail: /api/run spawns a pipeline on every POST (line 2689) with no check for an already-running run, no per-user limit, and no global cap. Each pipeline is expensive (many LLM calls, pandoc, two xelatex passes). Repeated clicks or scripted POSTs spawn unlimited concurrent pipelines, exhausting CPU/memory/API quota. Combined with the lack of auth, this is a trivial resource-exhaustion DoS. Hosting requires an admission queue and per-tenant concurrency limits.

issues.title: File-based JSONL IPC has no locking; SIGCHLD/preexec_fn hack locks design to single-threaded POSIX
issues.detail: Interview answers are appended with a plain open('a').write and no lock (_post_answer, line 2579), and taxonomy/qa state are read/written as bare files. This is safe only because the server is single-threaded and single-user; under any concurrency (or if the pipeline reads mid-write) records interleave or tear. Separately, the global signal.signal(SIGCHLD, SIG_IGN) (line 2587) plus the per-spawn preexec_fn reset (line 2527) is a fragile POSIX-fork-only mechanism: preexec_fn is not thread-safe and unsupported off fork platforms, so adopting a threaded/async server (needed for scale) would break the child-reaping workaround. The IPC layer should move to a real queue/DB with atomic writes.

issues.title: Unbounded POST body read enables trivial memory-exhaustion DoS
issues.detail: do_POST reads the entire request body into memory with self.rfile.read(int(Content-Length)) (lines 2681-2682) and no size limit. An attacker (no auth required) can send a multi-GB Content-Length on /api/qa/answer or /api/run and exhaust server memory; on a single-threaded server this also blocks all other clients during the read. Needs a max-body limit and streaming/early rejection.

strengths: /api/keys (lines 2659-2672) returns only presence booleans, never key values — correct minimal disclosure for the secrets-status surface.
Pipelines are spawned with start_new_session=True (line 2523) so a server restart or Ctrl-C does not kill in-flight runs — a sensible isolation choice for a long-running operator tool.
ETag/304 conditional responses (_json_response, lines 2596-2608) reduce redundant payload transfer to polling clients.
Defensive try/except around every artifact load (e.g. _load_state, _load_stage_artifacts) means one corrupt JSON file degrades gracefully instead of 500-ing the whole dashboard.
Default 127.0.0.1 bind (line 2763) is the correct safe default for the current personal-tool scope, even though it is the only thing standing between the app and the unauthenticated attack surface.
production_gaps: No authentication/authorization, sessions, or user accounts — anyone reaching the port has full control.
No CSRF tokens or Origin/Referer validation on state-changing POSTs; vulnerable to cross-site POST and DNS-rebinding against the localhost bind.
No run-scoped or tenant-scoped routing — a single global 'active' run is shared by all clients; concurrent runs/users collide.
No HTTPS/TLS; any deployment beyond localhost transmits everything (and any future key posts) in cleartext.
No input-path or directory sandboxing — /api/files enumerates the whole filesystem and /api/run ingests arbitrary host paths; /api/section traverses to arbitrary .md files.
No output escaping / HTML sanitization — source-document and LLM content is rendered via innerHTML and raw markdown, allowing stored XSS.
No concurrency control: single-threaded server, no request size limits, no run admission queue or per-user resource caps — trivial DoS.
No real-time transport (SSE/websocket); 2s full-file polling re-reads unbounded events.jsonl per client per cycle.
No robust process supervision — PID-file-only control with PID-reuse hazards, stale-file false positives, and no orphan reconciliation on restart.
No audit logging or rate limiting (log_message is suppressed, line 2611) — no record of who launched/stopped runs or read files.
Frontend is an inline Python string with no build/test/lint pipeline — cannot be safely evolved or security-reviewed in isolation.
Documented 'set keys via web UI (session only)' feature is unimplemented (README line 296) — intent-vs-code mismatch to resolve.
code.summary: observe.py is a competent single-user, localhost operator console accidentally being measured against a multi-tenant hosted product, and the gap is structural rather than cosmetic. Its core data model — one global 'active' run resolved by mtime, served by a single-threaded http.server with no auth, no CSRF, file-based IPC, and a 2s full-file polling loop — cannot support concurrent users without a ground-up redesign around run-scoped, authenticated routing. Security is the most acute layer: zero authn/authz on destructive endpoints, arbitrary filesystem enumeration (/api/files), .md path traversal (/api/section), arbitrary-input ingestion (/api/run), and stored XSS via unsanitized term names and markdown are all reachable today and gated only by the 127.0.0.1 bind. To become a hosted UI it needs auth + CSRF + TLS, per-run/per-tenant isolation, path/input sandboxing, output sanitization, a concurrent server with SSE/websocket push and incremental log tailing, supervised process management replacing the PID file, and the frontend extracted from the Python string into a testable codebase.

verdicts.reasoning: Every factual assertion verified against /Users/cyan/ccr/know-expand/know_expand/observe.py. Line 2763 is plain http.server.HTTPServer (single-threaded, serialized requests). Line 1464 is setInterval(poll, 2000), and each cycle actually hits FOUR endpoints (/api/status, /api/events, /api/qa, /api/taxonomy) plus /api/stage/:id every 5th poll — the claim understates request volume. _load_events (line 2387) reads and parses the entire events.jsonl per call with no tailing. _load_state (lines 2080-2099) re-parses the full events.jsonl on every /api/status once taxonomy.json exists. _load_stage_artifacts re-parses it again in the S5 (2226-2247), S6 (2286-2305), S8 (2338-2348), and S9 (2353+) branches. The ETag check (line 2599) compares If-None-Match only AFTER json.dumps builds the full payload (line 2597), so it saves bandwidth, not read/parse/serialize cost — and during an active run the events ETag changes nearly every poll, so full payloads are re-sent every 2s per tab. emit() in state.py appends unboundedly with no rotation; LLM-call and SS request events produce thousands of lines per deep run. Repo-wide search found zero mitigation: no ThreadingHTTPServer/ThreadingMixIn, no mtime caching, no lru_cache, no SSE/websocket. _render_section (line 2400) also does synchronous markdown rendering inside the single-threaded handler, making the "one slow handler blocks the QA poll" mechanism structurally real. The only soft spot is the saturation prediction: events lines are small (~100-300 bytes), so typical runs produce low-MB files where 1-2 tabs stay responsive; true saturation requires a long deep run (10+ MB) plus multiple tabs. Severity 'high' is at the upper bound for a localhost single-operator dashboard, but is defensible because the degradation directly hits the latency-sensitive QA interview poll (the only human-in-the-loop path, S1/S3) and per-poll cost provably grows O(file size) with no cap.

There is NO allowlist, NO confinement to runs_dir, NO is_relative_to/jail check anywhere in the function. It iterates target.iterdir() and, for each non-dotfile entry, appends {name, type, path (str(p) = absolute path), size} (lines 2432-2437). It also returns the resolved cwd and parent (line 2442). This matches the claim's description verbatim — name, type, absolute path, and size are all disclosed.

2. The route handler (lines 2653-2657) passes the raw `dir` query param straight into _list_files with no validation: `qs.get("dir", ["."])[0]` -> `_list_files(dir_param)`.

The only mitigating factor is that the server binds to 127.0.0.1 (line 2763), not 0.0.0.0, so it is not directly network-exposed by default. That tempers — but does not eliminate — the risk: the project is documented and tooled as a hostable dashboard that would normally sit behind nginx on a shared/hosted box (the auditor's stated threat model), and a localhost service is still reachable via reverse-proxy fronting, SSRF, or browser-driven CSRF/DNS-rebinding. The localhost bind is a deployment-level mitigation, not a code-level fix, and does not address the underlying defect.

The code-level vulnerability — unconfined, user-controlled filesystem enumeration that should be confined to runs_dir — is real, present, and exactly as described, including its value as reconnaissance for the companion .md traversal. The auditor's required remediation (confine to runs_dir) is correct and absent from the code.

This is a deployment mitigation only; the code defect (no runs_dir jail in _list_files) is fully real and unmitigated, and on the proxied/multi-tenant deployment the claim assumes, the high rating is appropriate.

verdicts.title: Path traversal in /api/section reads arbitrary .md files outside the run dir
verdicts.reasoning:
The cited code is quoted accurately: at /Users/cyan/ccr/know-expand/know_expand/observe.py:2636-2638 the handler does `sid = self.path[len("/api/section/"):].split("?")[0].strip("/")` then `path = state_dir / "sections" / f"section_{sid}.md"` and passes it unmodified to `_render_section` (lines 2400-2409), which calls `path.exists()` and `path.read_text()`. There is no realpath/containment check and `.resolve()` is never called. The `BaseHTTPRequestHandler`-doesn't-normalize-`..` observation is also true.

However, the core exploitability claim is FALSE because the auditor reasons about path traversal lexically (like os.path.normpath) instead of how the OS filesystem actually resolves paths. The `section_` prefix is f-string-concatenated to the FIRST component of sid, so any traversal payload produces a first extra component of literally `section_..` (e.g. for the auditor's own example /api/section/../../../../Users/victim/secret the path becomes .../sections/section_../../../../Users/victim/secret.md). The kernel resolves paths left-to-right against REAL directories: to apply a `..` it must first enter the preceding directory. A directory literally named `section_..` does not exist on disk, so the very first lookup returns ENOENT and `.exists()`/`open()` fail before any `..` is ever applied. I empirically verified this: every traversal variant I tried (`../`, `x/../`, the auditor's exact `../../../../Users/victim/secret`, double-slash to strip leading separators, 8x `..`) returns exists=False / FileNotFoundError. The auditor's claim that the "`section_` prefix only consumes one `..` level" is the specific error — `section_..` is a single non-existent directory name, not `section_` followed by a separate `..`.

The only way to escape would be for sid to begin with a path separator (making the first component `section_` followed by a fresh `/../`), but the handler's `.strip("/")` removes leading slashes, and even an embedded slash still yields `section_<first>` as a literal component that must exist on disk. S10 (s10_assemble.py:438,450) only ever writes `section_{domain_id}.md` FILES into the sections dir, never `section_*` subdirectories, so no real `section_<X>` directory exists to chain `..` through. There is therefore no arbitrary-.md-read and no filesystem-structure oracle via this endpoint. Severity high is unjustified; the practical exploitability is nil for the documented/normal deployment.

Caveat for honesty: this relies on POSIX-style on-disk resolution; the `section_` prefix is what saves it, not any deliberate validation, and a future change that created `section_*` directories or removed the prefix would reopen the issue. Adding an explicit realpath containment check would still be defensible hardening — but as written and deployed, the claimed vulnerability does not function.
verdicts.correction: The endpoint cannot read arbitrary .md files outside the run dir. Because the run-dir path component is built as `section_{sid}` via f-string, every traversal payload yields a first extra path component of literally `section_..` (or `section_<x>`), which is a directory that does not exist on disk. OS-level path resolution (used by Path.exists()/read_text(), the only resolution in the real code — `.resolve()` is never called) requires each `..` to be applied against a real existing directory, so the lookup fails with ENOENT before any `..` escapes the sections dir. I verified the auditor's own example path /api/section/../../../../Users/victim/secret produces .../sections/section_../../../../Users/victim/secret.md and returns FileNotFoundError. S10 only writes `section_*.md` files (never `section_*` directories) into the sections dir, so there is no real directory to chain traversal through. The auditor's verdict appears to be based on lexical normpath reasoning rather than actual filesystem behavior. An explicit realpath containment check remains reasonable defense-in-depth, but no arbitrary-file read or path-traversal exists as the code currently stands.

verdicts.title: Stored XSS: unescaped term names and unsanitized markdown HTML rendered via innerHTML
verdicts.reasoning:
All technical sinks are verified accurate. Line 1129 injects term names (from terms.json, extracted from the source document) raw into innerHTML with no escaping. Line 1290 sets view.innerHTML = d.html from the server. Line 2400 _render_section calls markdown.markdown() with no sanitizer; I empirically confirmed python-markdown passes <script> and onerror= through verbatim (markdown>=3.6 is a declared dependency, so the path is live). There is no JS-side escape helper anywhere; textContent is used only for static stage names. The other cited sinks (domain labels 1145/1204/1225, gap descriptions 1165, summary previews) likewise inject LLM/source-derived strings raw. There is no auth, no CSRF token, and no CSP, and the /api/run, /api/stop, and /api/files endpoints are reachable same-origin. So the vulnerability class (stored DOM XSS via unescaped term names + unsanitized markdown HTML) is real and reproducible.

However, the claim's severity rests on a 'hosted product' / remote-attacker premise that the code refutes: the server binds to 127.0.0.1 only (line 2763), with no --host flag and no 0.0.0.0 bind anywhere. This is a single-user local observability tool (CLAUDE.md: 'web UI at http://localhost:7842'). A remote/network attacker cannot reach the dashboard, and same-origin policy stops external sites from reading localhost responses. The realistic exploit is a local stored XSS requiring the victim to run serve, ingest an attacker-supplied document, and open the affected pane — at which point the payload runs same-origin and can drive the unauthenticated endpoints (genuine local file-read/pipeline-control impact). That is a real bug worth fixing, but materially narrower than the claimed remote hosted-product compromise, so 'high' is somewhat inflated for the as-shipped tool.
verdicts.correction: The XSS sinks and lack of escaping/sanitization are correct and empirically verified, and the recommended fix (output escaping + markdown sanitization, e.g. bleach/nh3) is sound. But the 'high' severity is inflated by a 'hosted product / remote attacker' framing the code does not support: the dashboard binds to 127.0.0.1 only (observe.py:2763) with no host-override flag, so it is a single-user local tool, not a network-exposed service. A remote attacker cannot reach it. The realistic threat is a local stored XSS that requires the victim to run serve, process an attacker-supplied document, and view the Extract/section pane; once triggered it does run same-origin and can call the unauthenticated /api/run, /api/stop, and /api/files endpoints (real local file-read/control impact). For the as-shipped local deployment this is closer to medium severity.

verdicts.title: /api/run accepts an arbitrary input path with no validation, becoming a file-read-to-output primitive
verdicts.reasoning:
The code-level mechanism is exactly as described. do_POST /api/run (observe.py:2688-2689) forwards the raw client JSON into _spawn_pipeline, which reads params.get("input") (line 2497) and places it unvalidated into the Popen args list as the document path (line 2510). S0 ingest (s0_ingest.py:71-72 does Path(input_path); line 125 does source_path.read_text(); line 77 docling-converts PDFs) reads any existing local file and writes its contents into source.txt/chunks, which are surfaced via /api/section/:id and the PDF output. There is NO allowlist, sandbox, uploads-confinement, authentication, or per-user authorization anywhere in observe.py or the codebase (grep for upload/allowlist/sandbox/auth/tenant returns nothing). The claim's note that args are a Popen list (no shell injection) is also correct. So the literal data-flow assertions are all true.

However, the SEVERITY (high) and the threat model are materially inflated/misframed. The entire claim rests on "exfiltration channel on a shared host," "other tenants' docs," and "no per-user authorization tying the input to the requester." But: (1) the server binds to 127.0.0.1 ONLY (observe.py:2763), so it is not reachable by other users or hosts — there is no shared-host/multi-tenant attack surface. (2) The system has no concept of users, tenants, or requesters at all; "no per-user authorization" describes a non-existent boundary, not a missing control. The README consistently frames serve as a single-user localhost:7842 dashboard. (3) The "arbitrary file read" reduces to: the single local operator can make the pipeline ingest a file they could already read directly with cat — no privilege escalation, no crossing of a trust boundary. It would only become a genuine vuln under an unmentioned CSRF/drive-by scenario (a malicious page POSTing to localhost), and even then results stay local, making real exfiltration non-trivial. The mechanism is confirmed; the high severity and "shared host / tenant exfiltration" framing are not supported by the actual loopback-bound, no-auth, single-user design.
verdicts.correction: The cited code does pass the client-supplied input path unvalidated into the CLI/ingest, and there is no allowlist/sandbox/auth — that part is accurate. But the severity should be low (not high) and the threat model is wrong: the server binds to 127.0.0.1 only (observe.py:2763), so there is no shared-host or multi-tenant exposure and no per-user boundary to violate. The system has no users/tenants by design; the operator reading an arbitrary local file via the pipeline gains nothing they could not already do by reading the file directly. It is only a meaningful issue under an unmentioned CSRF/drive-by vector (malicious web page POSTing to localhost:7842), for which hardening would be input-path confinement plus a CSRF token / Origin check — not "uploads area per user."

code.summary: The test suite (183 tests, all passing in ~19s) is real but badly skewed: it deeply covers pure string helpers and a few mocked stage flows while leaving the delivery-critical surfaces — observe.py (2,768 lines, 16 endpoints), pipeline wiring, CLI/SIGTERM, resume semantics, the PDF build, and most of the router fallback matrix — at zero coverage, and one stage test silently makes live HTTP calls to Wikipedia/PyPI/arXiv/OpenAlex. Delivery infrastructure is essentially absent for the stated production goal: the checked-in docker-compose.yml is a dead artifact from the doc-expand era (services the README itself rejects, `build: .` with no Dockerfile), the wheel is not actually installable because config.yaml/models.yaml are CWD-relative and not packaged, there is no CI, no release process, and — most importantly for a product whose deliverable is generated text — no output-quality eval harness of any kind.
strengths: 183 tests pass deterministically in 19s with no external test runner config needed (pytest settings in pyproject.toml, asyncio_mode=auto); LLM calls in stage tests are properly mocked via AsyncMock routers so no test depends on API keys.

Several tests encode real, specific past regressions rather than padding: tests/test_base.py:242-290 pins the geminicli _PROBED_UNAVAILABLE key-mismatch fix (commit fd18d6e), the _instructor_mode matrix (test_base.py:361-394) pins the Mistral/Groq/Gemini JSON-mode workarounds, and test_base.py:101-112 covers Anthropic cache_control blocks in _msg_chars.

Stage tests consistently verify the two invariants that matter for resume: skip-when-complete idempotency (s4_audit, s5_research, s7_synthesize, s8_verify, s10_assemble each have one) and per-domain failure isolation (tests/test_s3_integration.py:272-336, tests/test_s4_research.py:178).
tests/test_bibliography.py uses pytest-httpx (httpx_mock) correctly for hermetic Semantic Scholar API tests — the right pattern exists in the repo, it just isn't applied everywhere.

uv.lock is checked in (reproducible dev environment), the console entry point (know-expand = know_expand.cli:main) works, .gitignore correctly excludes .env and runs/, and the project LICENSE is MIT with an all-permissive dependency tree (docling/spacy/litellm/instructor/langgraph MIT, sentence-transformers Apache-2.0, pypdf/httpx BSD) — no copyleft contamination.

issues.title: Package is not actually pip-installable: config files are CWD-relative and not shipped in the wheel
issues.detail: know_expand/config.py:116-121 defaults load_config() to Path("config.yaml") / Path("models.yaml") resolved against the current working directory, and know_expand/cli.py:159 calls load_config() with no arguments. config.yaml and models.yaml live at the repo root, outside the know_expand package, so the hatchling wheel (pyproject.toml:1-3) will not include them. Result: `pip install know-expand && know-expand paper.pdf` fails with FileNotFoundError from any directory except a repo checkout. Compounding this, LlamaCppConfig hardcodes a private LAN IP as the library default (know_expand/config.py:70: base_url="http://192.168.1.117:8080") — a personal-machine artifact baked into shipped defaults. For a product 'many users run', the entry point only works for the author.

issues.title: docker-compose.yml is a dead artifact from the doc-expand era; README documents a different, also-nonexistent deployment
issues.detail: docker-compose.yml:1-35 defines grobid, anystyle, and phoenix services — zero references to any of them exist in know_expand/ or config.yaml (verified by grep), and README.md:889 explicitly lists 'Phoenix/Langfuse as Docker service' as a rejected alternative. The compose network is still named doc_expand (docker-compose.yml:7, pre-rename), the app service uses `build: .` but there is no Dockerfile anywhere in the repo, and the volumes (./state, ./output, docker-compose.yml:47-49) do not match the actual runs/{run_id}/state|logs|output layout. issues.title: Test suite is not hermetic: s4_audit integration tests make live HTTP calls to OpenAlex/Wikipedia/PyPI/arXiv
issues.detail: tests/test_s3_integration.py:186-189 and 309-314 patch fetch_anchors/fetch_bibliography/fetch_anchor_neighbors/make_router but NOT fetch_sources_for_terms, which s4_audit.run() invokes unconditionally (know_expand/stages/s4_audit.py:232,251). Every test run issues real network requests for the fixture terms 'Alpha'/'Beta'/'Gamma'. The suite only passes offline because sources.py swallows every exception into debug logs (know_expand/sources.py:292-294, 346-348) — i.e., the network dependency is masked, not absent. Smoking gun: the observed RuntimeWarning during the run ('AsyncLimiter instance is being re-used across loops' at know_expand/sources.py:314) proves _fetch_openalex_works executed inside the 'fully mocked' test. That warning also exposes a latent production bug: the module-level cached _OPENALEX_LIMITER (sources.py:40-46) is reused across event loops, which aiolimiter documents as undefined behavior — relevant the moment multiple runs share a process.

issues.title: No CI/CD, no lint, no type-check, no coverage measurement — quality gates do not exist
issues.detail: There is no .github/ directory (verified), no workflow files, no Makefile/tox/nox, and the dev extra (pyproject.toml:39-44) contains only pytest, pytest-asyncio, and pytest-httpx — no ruff, no mypy, no pytest-cov, despite .gitignore:211 listing .ruff_cache/ (tooling was apparently used ad hoc and never committed as config). Nothing runs the 183 tests automatically; the commit message claiming '182 tests' (3df1514) is already stale (183 collected), which is exactly the drift CI would catch. For a multi-user product, every merge to main is currently unverified.

issues.title: The product's actual deliverable — generated long-form text and a PDF — has zero quality evaluation
issues.detail: The value of know-expand is the quality of LLM-generated research prose, citations, and the assembled PDF. None of that is evaluated anywhere: there is no eval harness, no golden input document with expected-output regression, no rubric/LLM-judge scoring, no citation-accuracy benchmark, and no fixtures directory (verified by find). All LLM interactions in tests are canned Pydantic objects (e.g. tests/test_s4_research.py:38-63), so prompt changes — the highest-churn, highest-risk surface, e.g. the 1,017-line s5_research.py — can silently degrade output with no signal. Even the deterministic end of delivery is untested: the pandoc + double-xelatex path (a 'non-negotiable' invariant per CLAUDE.md) is only exercised via its skip branch (tests/test_s7_assemble.py:165 test_s7_pdf_skip_when_pandoc_unavailable); no test ever produces a PDF. A judgment that 'the build is green' currently says nothing about whether the product output got better or worse.

issues.title: Coverage is heavily skewed: 38% of all tests target two string helpers while observe.py, pipeline.py, cli.py, and 6 of 11 stages have zero tests
issues.detail: tests/test_s10_pdf.py contains 70 of the 183 tests (38%), all for _fix_bare_math and _sanitize_bib_entry — two pure string functions in s10_assemble. Meanwhile: observe.py (2,768 lines — 24% of the codebase — 16 HTTP endpoints, the qa/taxonomy IPC protocol, SIGCHLD handling, subprocess spawning) has zero tests; pipeline.py (LangGraph wiring), cli.py (including the SIGTERM-emits-run_stopped invariant listed in CLAUDE.md's 'Important constraints'), and state.py's emit() are untested; stages s0_ingest, s1_assess (interview IPC), s2_extract, s3_graph (taxonomy review IPC), s6_align, and s9_prereq have no tests at all. The router fallback matrix documented in CLAUDE.md has 5 rows but tests cover only 3 — the Retry-After exact-sleep path, the headerless 429 exponential backoff (2s/4s/8s), and the 3-consecutive-failures permanent skip (know_expand/agents/base.py:726-930, notably duplicated in two near-identical copies) are all untested. The two human-in-the-loop IPC protocols and the resume mechanism — the features most likely to break under concurrent multi-user load — are precisely the untested ones.

issues.title: Undeclared direct runtime dependencies: PyYAML and langchain-core
issues.detail: know_expand/config.py:4 does `import yaml` and know_expand/agents/lc_adapter.py:17-26 imports langchain_core directly, but pyproject.toml:9-34 declares neither PyYAML nor langchain-core. Both currently resolve only transitively (via litellm/docling and langgraph respectively). A routine upstream dependency refactor would break a fresh install of this package with ImportError at startup — config loading is the first thing cli.py does. This is exactly the class of breakage a lockfile does not protect end users from, since pip consumers install from pyproject metadata, not uv.lock.

issues.title: Every stage test file is named for the pre-rename stage numbering — systematic off-by-rename drift
issues.detail: After the stage renumbering (audit inserted at S4, etc.), no test file was renamed: tests/test_s3_integration.py tests s4_audit (its own docstring at line 2 still says 'Stage 3 (Anchored Audit)' while line 218-219 asserts stages['4']), test_s4_research.py tests s5_research, test_s5_synthesize.py tests s7_synthesize, test_s6_verify.py tests s8_verify, and test_s7_assemble.py/test_s10_pdf.py test s10_assemble. Function names compound it (test_s3_run_writes_outputs..., test_s4_writes_section..., test_s6_detects_needs_citation for s8_verify). Anyone triaging a failure in 'test_s6_verify' will open s6_align.py first. Pure rename debt, but it makes the suite actively misleading and CI failure output unreadable.

issues.title: No release/versioning machinery: 0.1.0 forever, no tags, no changelog, bare project metadata
issues.detail: pyproject.toml:7 pins version="0.1.0" across all 64 commits; the repo has zero git tags (verified), no CHANGELOG, and know_expand/__init__.py carries no __version__. The [project] table omits license, readme, classifiers, urls, and description even though a LICENSE file (MIT) and a 59KB README exist — so a published wheel would surface as anonymous metadata on PyPI. System-level runtime requirements are also undeclared and unenforced: spacy's en_core_web_sm (a hard constraint per CLAUDE.md) appears nowhere in pyproject or uv.lock, and pandoc/xelatex/node(npx for geminicli) have no preflight documentation beyond prose. A new user's first run fails on a missing spaCy model with no install-time hint.

issues.title: Delivery infrastructure assumes a single developer machine, contradicting the multi-user production goal
issues.detail: Everything in the delivery layer is single-tenant: config resolution from CWD (config.py:116-121), runs/ rooted in the repo directory, the serve process is documented (README.md:828) as the sole observability surface with no auth/health-check/container story, and the cheapest model tier (geminicli) depends on a personal OAuth token at ~/.gemini/oauth_creds.json driving the free gemini-cli quota — per-developer-machine state that cannot be shipped to concurrent users and is at best ToS-grey for a hosted product (per-user personal quota repurposed as product capacity). There is no horizontal story at all: no image, no process supervisor, no queue, no per-tenant isolation of runs/. For SaaS or even serious self-hosting, the delivery architecture has to be designed, not patched.

production_gaps: No Dockerfile and no working container path — the checked-in docker-compose.yml cannot start (references a Dockerfile that does not exist and services from the abandoned doc-expand architecture); README's Deployment section describes a compose file that is not in the repo.
No CI pipeline of any kind (.github/ absent): tests, lint, type-check, and packaging are never verified automatically; no coverage measurement exists so the severe coverage skew is invisible.

No output-quality eval harness: no golden documents, no citation-accuracy or hallucination regression checks, no LLM-judge or rubric scoring — prompt changes ship blind even though generated text is the entire product.

Wheel is broken for end users: config.yaml/models.yaml are not packaged and are resolved relative to CWD, so the installed console script only works from a repo checkout; PyYAML and langchain-core are undeclared dependencies.

System dependencies unmanaged: spaCy en_core_web_sm, pandoc, xelatex, and node/npx (for geminicli) are required at runtime but appear in no dependency metadata, preflight check at install time, or container image.

Tests issue live third-party HTTP requests (OpenAlex/Wikipedia/PyPI/arXiv) from the 'mocked' s4_audit integration tests — flaky offline/air-gapped and rude to upstream APIs under CI parallelism; no network-isolation marker or socket-blocking fixture.
No release process: version frozen at 0.1.0, zero git tags, no CHANGELOG, no PyPI metadata (license/classifiers/urls/readme undeclared); referenced .env.example file does not exist.

No load or concurrency testing for the serve process and its file-based IPC (qa_queue.jsonl, taxonomy_choice.json, pipeline_pid) despite the goal of many concurrent users; observe.py's 16 endpoints have zero tests of any kind.

research.summary: The market splits into five clusters, none of which occupies know-expand's exact position. (1) Document-grounded study tools: Google NotebookLM (17M+ MAU, free to $99.99-200/mo via Google AI tiers, added its own Deep Research in Nov 2025 plus audio/video/slide outputs) and Anara/ex-Unriddle (claims 3M users, $10-20/mo, $167/mo Deep Search, passage-level citation verification). These produce interactive artifacts or short reports, never long verified documents. (2) Foundation-lab Deep Research features (OpenAI $20/$100/$200 tiers with 10/50/250 runs per month, Gemini, Claude, Perplexity at $20/mo with 45M users and ~$450M ARR): commodity 10-40 page web-sourced reports, no pedagogy, no verification pass, no bibliographic rigor. (3) Scientific literature tools: Elicit (2M+ users, $12-79/user/mo plus custom enterprise, PRISMA 2020 systematic-review product for pharma), Consensus (10M+ users, $30M Series A May 2026, $10-45/mo), SciSpace ($12-20/mo), Undermind ($16-20/mo, YC, 1,000+ GSK scientists), and Ai2's free open-source Asta agents on Semantic Scholar — these do search/screening/extraction, not synthesis into learning material. (4) Open source: Stanford STORM (70k preview users, short Wikipedia-style articles, research artifact) and gpt-researcher (27.4k GitHub stars, 5-10 page reports). (5) The closest analog on depth and pricing: Edison Scientific's Kosmos ($70M seed at $250M valuation; 12-hour autonomous runs reading ~1,500 papers producing fully-cited reports at $200/run) — but it targets discovery/hypothesis generation, not pedagogy. AI doc-to-course L&D tools (Coassemble, eduMe, Synthesia, eSkilled at $9-29/mo) produce shallow microlearning from internal docs, and Google's Learn Your Way/LearnLM personalizes existing textbooks rather than creating field guides from papers. WHITE SPACE: no product combines (a) 200+ page book-grade artifact, (b) citation verification/audit, (c) pedagogical structuring (reader profiling, prerequisites, worked examples), (d) seeded from one paper. Nobody is paying for that exact artifact yet because nobody sells it — but adjacent segments pay heavily for verified synthesized documents: pharma spends ~$141k per systematic literature review (~$16.8M/yr per top-10 pharma company); AlphaSense hit $600M ARR at a $7.5B valuation (June 2026) selling verified research synthesis to 7,000 enterprises; Hebbia ($161M raised) penetrated 33% of top asset managers for diligence document synthesis; expert networks are a ~$3B market growing toward ~$4.9B; corporate training is a $400B market with AI-powered training at $7.49B in 2026 and Sana (acquired by Workday) charging $50-100k/yr; Primer ($237M raised) sells traceable synthesis to defense/intel; and OpenEvidence ($12B valuation, used by 40%+ of US physicians) proves that citation-grounded domain synthesis can reach massive adoption when verification is the headline feature. The risk: deep-research output is commoditizing fast (NotebookLM bundling at $7.99/mo), so the defensible position is the verified, typeset, pedagogically-structured book — priced per artifact (Kosmos validates $200/run), sold into pharma medical affairs, consulting/PE technical diligence, defense/intel, and technical onboarding rather than to individual learners.

implications: The exact artifact know-expand produces — a 200+ page verified, pedagogically-structured, typeset field guide grown from one seed paper — has no direct competitor. Every adjacent tool stops at either short reports (Deep Research, STORM, gpt-researcher), interactive study aids (NotebookLM, Anara), search/extraction (Elicit, Consensus, Undermind, Asta), or discovery reports (Kosmos). The white space is real, but so is the reason it's empty: no proven consumer demand for book-length output, so validation must come from professional segments.

Do not price as a $10-20/mo subscription — that band is saturated (NotebookLM $7.99, Consensus $10, Elicit $12, SciSpace $12, Undermind $16, Perplexity/ChatGPT/Anara $20) and buys commodity reports. Kosmos's $200/run and Anara's $167/mo Deep Search tier validate per-artifact / premium pricing; a verified 200-page guide plausibly supports $100-500 per run, which also comfortably covers know-expand's token costs (relevant to the planned --batch-mode 50% discount).

Verification is the marketable moat, not generation. Anara wins users with passage-level citation links; OpenEvidence reached a $12B valuation on citation-grounded trust; Primer sells traceability to defense. know-expand's S8 citation audit, CSL-JSON bibliography, 65/35 foundational/frontier split, and [NEEDS_CITATION] discipline should be the headline of any positioning — and surfacing a per-claim 'verification report' alongside the PDF would make the moat visible.

The S1 interview and S3 human taxonomy review are differentiators, not friction: Google's Learn Your Way RCT showed personalization to the reader measurably improves outcomes, and no deep-research competitor profiles the reader at all. Keep human-in-the-loop as a premium feature rather than racing the fully-autonomous tools.

Best-paying wedges in order of evidence strength: (1) pharma medical affairs / literature review teams (~$141k per SLR, $16.8M/yr per top-10 pharma; Elicit Enterprise proves the buyer exists — a PRISMA-adjacent 'field guide' mode could ride the same budget); (2) consulting/PE technical due diligence (AlphaSense $600M ARR, Hebbia in 33% of top asset managers — a deep-tech diligence guide from a target's key patent/paper is a natural fit); (3) defense/intel analyst onboarding (Primer's segment; know-expand's provenance/event-log architecture fits the traceability requirement); (4) corporate technical onboarding L&D ($50-100k/yr Sana-style contracts; existing doc-to-course tools are shallow, leaving deep technical material unserved).

Commoditization is the main threat and it is fast: NotebookLM shipped Deep Research, 1M-token chat, and PPTX export within ~5 months and bundles at $7.99/mo. know-expand should not market itself as 'deep research' (a lost battle) but as 'the verified book' — output quality (xelatex typesetting, prerequisite primers, worked examples, boss-node synthesis) that chat products structurally won't replicate.

Free infrastructure is improving in know-expand's favor: Ai2's Asta/Semantic Scholar (already used for bibliography) and OpenAlex (already used for taxonomy validation) are open and grounded — the cost structure of the pipeline benefits while competitors who monetize search (Consensus, Undermind) get squeezed.

GTM pattern worth copying from Edison/Kosmos: a small free tier of full runs (they give 6 to academics) to let the artifact sell itself, since a 200-page verified guide is a demo that no screenshot conveys; pair with per-run pricing for individuals and seat/volume licensing for the pharma/consulting/defense segments.

research.summary: Current (June 2026) best practice for productionizing 1-3 hour multi-agent LangGraph pipelines converges on five layers: (1) durable execution — either LangGraph Platform (managed queues, Postgres checkpointing, background runs, webhooks, HITL interrupts at $39/mo + $0.001/node) or a durable-execution engine (Temporal for scale, DBOS/Hatchet for minimal-footprint Postgres-backed durability; the 2026 consensus is that most teams should start with the lightweight option and only adopt Temporal when they hit real scale); (2) interrupt-based human-in-the-loop with a Postgres checkpointer so paused runs survive process death, with idempotency required for any pre-interrupt side effects; (3) per-run/per-tenant cost metering via a proxy pattern (LiteLLM virtual keys with budgets and tag-based attribution is the de facto standard); (4) observability via Langfuse (MIT, self-hostable, ~1/3 the cost of LangSmith at volume) emitting OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic-convention attributes (still Development status — pin versions); (5) cost reduction via batch APIs — Anthropic and OpenAI both give a flat 50% discount with a 24h ceiling, and batch + prompt-caching discounts stack. Evals for long-form generated documents are now standard practice: versioned LLM-as-judge rubrics (with a human reference document to fight score saturation on long surveys) plus RAGAS/DeepEval faithfulness and citation-accuracy metrics in CI. A minimal production architecture for know-expand: keep the LangGraph pipeline self-hosted; swap pipeline.json-only resume for a real SQLite/Postgres checkpointer; replace file-based Q&A IPC with interrupt()/Command(resume=); route all LLM calls through a LiteLLM proxy with one virtual key per run for $-per-run accounting and hard budget caps; self-host Langfuse and map the existing emit()/events.jsonl to OTel gen_ai spans; ship --batch-mode on the Anthropic Batches API with 1-hour prompt-cache TTL and the planned s5_batch_poll event; add a DeepEval citation-faithfulness eval gate over S8 outputs. No Temporal Cloud or LangGraph Cloud spend is justified at single-user scale, but the architecture should keep stage boundaries activity-shaped so a later move to Hatchet/DBOS/Temporal is mechanical.

key_facts.fact: LangGraph Platform Plus tier: $39/month including 100k node executions, then $0.001 per node executed plus standby charges of $0.0007/min (dev) and $0.0036/min (prod). Provides hosted execution, built-in Postgres checkpointing, task queues, LangGraph Studio debugging, streaming, and webhooks. Developer tier is free with 5k traces/month.

LangGraph Platform's stated value proposition is out-of-the-box persistence, memory, double-texting handling, human-in-the-loop, cron scheduling, webhooks, background runs with polling/streaming/webhook monitoring, and support for long-running tasks — exactly the glue code know-expand currently hand-rolls in observe.py.

LangGraph's interrupt() pauses graph execution and saves state via the checkpointer; Command(resume=...) resumes it. PostgresSaver persists checkpoints across restarts and long pauses (MemorySaver is dev-only; SqliteSaver suits single-process deployments). The thread_id is the persistent cursor for resuming. Critical caveat: any logic before interrupt() (paid API calls, writes) must be idempotent because it re-runs on resume.

Temporal pattern for LLM apps: workflows are the deterministic orchestration layer, LLM calls and tool executions run as Activities with automatic retries and recovery. Replay 2026 added Serverless Workers, Standalone Activities, Workflow Streams, and Google ADK / OpenAI Agents SDK integrations.

Temporal Cloud pricing (2026): $50 per million Actions pay-as-you-go; Essentials plan from $100/month (1M actions, 99.9% SLA), Business from $500/month. Self-hosting is free but requires operating the Temporal server cluster.

DBOS provides durable execution as an in-process Python library backed only by Postgres — no separate orchestrator, history cluster, or queue daemon. The 2026 consensus: most backend services can ship durable execution with DBOS and move to Temporal only if they hit real scale walls; DBOS fits when side effects land in your own Postgres and throughput is a few thousand state transitions/sec.

Hatchet is an open-source orchestration engine whose durable tasks are positioned as a drop-in replacement for Temporal/DBOS workflows; teams choose it over Celery for native asyncio support — a significant Celery gap given long-lived LLM API calls. 2026 industry practice is to replace Celery entirely for multi-step workflows with Temporal or Hatchet.

Anthropic Message Batches API: 50% off input and output tokens on all models; a batch is limited to 100,000 requests or 256 MB; most batches finish under 1 hour with a hard 24-hour expiry ('expired' results are not billed); results downloadable for 29 days; no completion callback — you poll batch status (30s intervals are standard practice); max_tokens:0 cache pre-warming is unsupported in batches; docs recommend the 1-hour prompt-cache duration (not 5-min ephemeral) for shared context across batched requests; not ZDR-eligible.

OpenAI Batch API: flat 50% discount on all models, 24h completion window (not configurable), up to 50,000 requests per batch file, 2,000 batches/hour creation limit. Prompt caching and batch discounts stack — cached input on GPT-5.4 drops to $0.625/M, 75% off the standard $2.50 rate.

OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions remain in Development status as of May 2026 with no stabilization timeline. Key attributes: gen_ai.usage.input_tokens, gen_ai.usage.output_tokens, gen_ai.usage.cache_read.input_tokens (included within input_tokens), plus the gen_ai.client.token.usage metric. OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN=gen_ai_latest_experimental controls version transitions — pin conventions because attribute names may still change.

Langfuse is MIT-licensed with first-class self-hosting (Docker Compose in ~30 min); LangSmith self-hosting requires an Enterprise license. At 1M traces/month: Langfuse Cloud ~$919 vs LangSmith ~$2,500+; self-hosted Langfuse ~$150/month infra. Langfuse auto-computes per-call cost from model + token counts including cached-token usage types, with custom model pricing for self-hosted models.

LangSmith pricing: free Developer tier 5k traces/month, Plus at $39/seat/month with 10k base traces, overage $2.50/1k traces (14-day retention) or $5/1k (400-day). Best fit only for all-in LangChain/LangGraph shops wanting managed SaaS.

LiteLLM proxy is the de facto per-tenant metering layer: virtual keys are independently revocable with their own budgets (multiple budget windows, model-specific budgets), RPM/TPM limits, and allowed-model restrictions; spend is automatically tracked in Postgres for keys/users/teams across 100+ LLMs; tags attached to keys give per-customer/per-feature cost attribution with enforced tag budgets.

Multi-tenant LLM cost-governance best practice: attach tenant/user/task identifiers to every LLM request at creation time, route everything through a single proxy that normalizes and logs, set daily per-tenant spend caps with automated rate-limit tightening, and alert on per-tenant spend vs a 7-day rolling baseline. Streaming responses require incremental token accounting.

LLM-as-judge is the default 2026 eval method (~85% agreement with human reviewers, higher than human-human agreement), but rubric-only setups exhibit leniency and score saturation specifically on long-text survey generation; the fix is giving the judge a human-written reference document on the same topic alongside the generated text (SurveyEval). Datasets, rubrics, and judge models are versioned as strictly as code.

The three production-ready RAG/citation eval frameworks in 2026 are RAGAS, DeepEval, and Promptfoo. RAGAS faithfulness and DeepEval FaithfulnessEval are both production-grade (DeepEval has better claim decomposition in 2026 builds; RAGAS more battle-tested); DeepEval adds a citation-accuracy metric and pytest/CI integration, making it the choice for CI gates while RAGAS suits notebook/data-pipeline workflows.

The 2026 production reference architecture for durable LLM agents combines a durable-execution primitive with the LangGraph checkpointer model, a replay-safety contract, idempotency keys derived from workflow + step IDs for non-idempotent tool/LLM calls, and resumable SSE for streaming to UIs.

A worked example of running Anthropic's Message Batches API inside Temporal exists (submit batch as an activity, poll as a heartbeating activity, fetch results as a third activity) — the standard pattern for marrying 24h-window batch jobs with durable orchestration.

implications: Resume mechanism: pipeline.json stage markers are coarse (stage-level, not node-level) and lose all intra-stage work on crash. Adopt a LangGraph checkpointer — SqliteSaver is sufficient for the current single-process CLI (runs/{run_id}/state/checkpoint.db), PostgresSaver only if/when multi-instance. Keep pipeline.json markers as the human-readable fallback, but make the checkpointer the real resume path. Stage boundaries in pipeline.py are already activity-shaped, so a later lift to DBOS/Hatchet/Temporal is mechanical — do not buy Temporal Cloud ($100+/mo) or LangGraph Cloud at single-user scale.

Human-in-the-loop: the qa_queue.jsonl / qa_answers.jsonl / taxonomy_review.json file IPC should become interrupt() + Command(resume=...) on the checkpointer. This makes S1 interview and S3 taxonomy review survive process death (today a crash mid-interview loses the session), works identically for TTY and web, and removes the qa_complete sentinel-file race. Hard requirement from the docs: code before interrupt() re-runs on resume, so the S1 question-generation LLM call must be idempotent or cached — derive an idempotency key from run_id + stage + turn number.

Cost metering: replace ad-hoc accounting with a LiteLLM proxy instance and one virtual key per run. know-expand already speaks litellm SDK, so this is a base_url + api_key change in agents/base.py. A per-run key gives exact $-per-run attribution for the $1-150 range, a hard budget cap (kill a runaway deep run at e.g. $200), and per-provider rate limits that could eventually replace the hand-rolled per-provider semaphores. QuotaAwareRouter's fallback chain stays — the proxy complements, not replaces, it.

Observability: self-host Langfuse (Docker Compose) rather than LangSmith — LangSmith self-hosting is Enterprise-only and know-expand is not all-in on LangChain abstractions. Map emit() events to OTel gen_ai spans: llm_call_done already carries cache_read_tok, which maps directly to gen_ai.usage.cache_read.input_tokens. Because GenAI semconv is still Development status, pin the convention version and keep events.jsonl as the source of truth; treat Langfuse/OTel as a projection.

--batch-mode (planned, not yet implemented): the Anthropic Batches API design is confirmed viable — 50% off, 8 domains x 4 personas is far under the 100k-request/256MB limit, most batches finish <1h so the 1-3h wall-clock estimate is conservative. Three concrete requirements from the docs: (1) poll on ~30s intervals and emit the planned s5_batch_poll event each cycle; (2) switch the S5 shared-context cache_control from 5-minute ephemeral to the 1-hour cache duration, since ephemeral entries expire during batch processing; (3) handle the 'expired' result type (unbilled) by resubmitting those requests synchronously. Note batch mode is not ZDR-eligible if that ever matters.

Eval gate: add a DeepEval-based CI job over assembled outputs — citation-accuracy and faithfulness metrics against the cached audit/sources/*.json and CSL-JSON bibliography are a natural extension of S8 verify (which already does citation audit but with no regression baseline). For whole-document quality, run an LLM-as-judge with a versioned rubric AND a human-written reference survey on the same topic, because rubric-only judging demonstrably saturates on long-form survey text. research.summary:
Research across four areas (measured citation error rates, production faithfulness machinery, legal/reputational exposure, copyright of single-source derivatives) converges on one conclusion: 'check citation key exists in bibliography' is roughly level 1 of a 6-level verification ladder, and the gap between it and a defensible 'verified' claim is where all the documented failures live.

(1) MEASURED ERROR RATES. Plain LLMs asked for references remain unreliable: a 2025 Deakin University audit of GPT-4o literature reviews found 19.9% of 176 citations fully fabricated and 56% fabricated-or-erroneous, with fabrication spiking to ~30% on less-studied topics; Gemini fabrication fell from ~100% (2023) to ~12% (recent), showing improvement but not safety. A large-scale bibliometric audit found ~146,900 AI-generated fake citations in the 2025 scientific literature itself. Commercial deep-research products do better but are far from clean: citation accuracy spans 78% (OpenAI Deep Research) to 94% (Claude with search) under the FACT framework; Perplexity's DRACO benchmark (Feb 2026) shows the best system at only ~64.6% citation quality and ~67.9% factual accuracy — citation quality and factuality are the weakest axes. An April 2026 study (urlhealth, arXiv 2604.03173) measured 3–13% of cited URLs as outright hallucinated and 5–18% non-resolving across 10 systems and 220k+ URLs, with deep-research agents worse than search-augmented chat — but self-correction tooling cut bad citations 6–79× to under 1%, proving link/existence validation is cheap and automatable. The failure taxonomy matters: existence failures (reference doesn't exist), resolution failures (link rot), and faithfulness failures (real source doesn't support the claim) are distinct, and the third survives all bibliography-level checks.

(2) PRODUCTION FAITHFULNESS MACHINERY. The state of practice is layered: (a) retrieval-grounded generation so references come from real indexes (Semantic Scholar/OpenAlex-grounded tools achieve >90% citation accuracy vs <60% for free-generation LLMs); (b) claim-level attribution at generation time — Anthropic's Citations API (GA on API and Vertex since early 2025) returns character-level pointers from each output claim to source passages; (c) post-hoc verification via atomic-claim decomposition + NLI/LLM entailment against retrieved evidence — the FActScore/SAFE/VeriScore family, sped up by VeriFastScore; production detectors like Vectara's HHEM score grounded-summarization consistency; (d) reference-resolution tooling (urlhealth) and citation-context classification (Scite's supports/mentions/contradicts model). Research (Wallat et al. 2024/25) adds a caution: 'correctness is not faithfulness' — a real, even relevant citation can still be decorative if the model never used it; current best practice verifies entailment, not provenance.

(3) LEGAL/REPUTATIONAL EXPOSURE. Selling error-laden 'research-grade' AI documents has already produced concrete losses: Deloitte Australia refunded the final installment of a A$440k (~US$290k) government report after a researcher found fabricated academic references and a fake court quote (Oct 2025), then faced a second incident on a ~C$1.6M Newfoundland report (Nov 2025); the White House MAHA report (May 2025) was caught with at least 7 nonexistent studies and 'oaicite' markers, requiring public correction; Damien Charlotin's tracker logged 1,200+ court decisions involving AI-hallucinated citations by early 2026 (>1,597 by June 2026), with ≥$145k in US sanctions in Q1 2026 alone. On the regulatory side, the FTC's Operation AI Comply (DoNotPay: $193k settlement plus consumer notices for overclaiming an AI legal product's capabilities) establishes that marketing an AI product as 'verified'/'research-grade' without substantiation is itself an actionable deceptive claim, independent of any individual error.

(4) COPYRIGHT OF SINGLE-SOURCE DERIVATIVES. A knowledge expansion generated from one source paper is presumptively a derivative work of that paper. The US Copyright Office's May 2025 report says transformativeness is 'a matter of degree' and uses that compete with or substitute for the original are disfavored; Thomson Reuters v. Ross (Feb 2025, first AI fair-use ruling) rejected fair use where the AI product served a substitutional commercial market; Wainwright Securities v. Wall Street Transcript (2d Cir. 1977) is direct precedent that systematic abstracts/summaries of analytical reports infringe. Mitigating factors for a pedagogical expansion: it serves learners rather than replacing the paper for its research audience, most expansion content is newly synthesized from third-party sources rather than reproduced, and many inputs are openly licensed (CC BY) — but arXiv's default non-exclusive license does NOT permit derivatives, and CC BY-NC-ND inputs bar commercial derivatives outright, so license-aware input gating is required. Anthropic's $1.5B Bartz settlement and publisher/STM disclosure taxonomies signal a hardening environment: disclose AI generation, respect source licenses, avoid verbatim reproduction.

CONCLUSION — QUALITY BAR AND THE GAP. The verification ladder is: L1 citation key resolves in bibliography (pure referential integrity); L2 reference exists in the world with matching metadata (DOI/SS ID, authors, year, title); L3 link/DOI resolves (urlhealth-class checks); L4 claim–source topical relevance; L5 claim-level entailment — each cited sentence decomposed into atomic claims and verified as supported by the actual source text/abstract via NLI or LLM-judge, with unsupported claims repaired, removed, or visibly flagged in the deliverable; L6 calibration + sampled human audit + provenance/AI-use disclosure. A paid 'verified knowledge expansion' product needs, at minimum: 100% L2/L3 (fully automatable, near-zero cost — the urlhealth result shows <1% residual is achievable), >95% L5 support rate measured by an independent entailment pass with the residual visibly flagged (matching the >90% bar of source-grounded tools and clearly beating the ~65% DRACO ceiling of general deep-research products), per-document verification reports the buyer can audit, AI-use disclosure, and substantiation records for the word 'verified' (FTC exposure). 'Citation key exists in bibliography' is L1: it catches typos and dangling keys, and catches exactly zero of the failure modes documented above — every fabricated Deloitte reference, every MAHA phantom study, and every unsupported-claim citation would pass it. The honest distance is four full ladder levels, though a Semantic Scholar-grounded bibliography (as know-expand already has) structurally buys L2 for SS-sourced entries, leaving claim-level entailment (L5) as the real engineering frontier.

points.title: BEAR 2 — The headline claim is false today, and 'verified' is now a legally actionable word
